verses.13: Unlike the psalmist’s earlier request that God stay close to him (38:21-22), his present desire for God to "leave" him "alone" echoes Job’s disposition (Job 7:17-19).
verses.1-13: This prayer for rescue reflects the psalmist’s discouragement, which comes from having a limited perspective on his situation.
verses.1-3: Suffering in "silence" only intensifies the psalmist’s anguish, pain, and inner "turmoil".
verses.4-6: Because of his suffering and sin, the psalmist concludes that life is meaningless and fleeting (see Job 7:7-10; Isa 40:6-8). He had expected a wicked life to have those qualities (see Pss 37:2, 20; 103:15-16), but now whether a person is godly or not seems to be irrelevant.
verses.4-5: "how fleeting my life is:" This perspective comes out of suffering (see 78:39; 89:47-48; 90:3-10). The human "lifetime" is but a "moment" to God (90:4), as temporary as a "breath" (see 39:11; 144:4).
verses.9-11: The psalmist links suffering with God’s "discipline", assuming that it is "punishment" for his sin.

verses.6: The Lord delights in the attitude and character of the person making an offering more than in the offering itself. • "Now that you have made me listen, I finally understand:" Greek text reads You have given me a body. In Heb 10:5-7, the writer quotes from the Greek version of Ps 40:6-8. He casts the words as something Jesus said as he left heaven and came into the world.
verses.7: "As is written about me in the Scriptures:" Moses had recorded God’s requirements for Israel’s kings in Deut 17:14-15.
verses.11: The psalmist prays that the Lord will be true to his character when answering this plea for mercy.
verses.1-17: This psalm includes a thanksgiving song (40:1-10) followed by a lament (40:11-17). The thanksgiving song includes the reason for the thanksgiving (40:1-5), an affirmation of commitment (40:6-8), and a public testimony of God’s character (40:7-10). The lament concerns the psalmist’s troubles because of his sins (40:11-12) and is followed by two prayers for vindication (40:13-15, 17).
verses.1-5: The psalmist thanks the Lord for his rescue and testifies that God can be trusted.
verses.12-17: The psalmist is troubled by both his adversities and his own "sins" and prays for rescue. • This passage is repeated almost verbatim as Ps 70.

verses.1: The "poor" who suffer hardship have special protection under God’s law (Lev 14:21; 19:10); they receive God’s justice and godly rule (Pss 72:13; 82:3-4). The word translated poor is often a synonym for the godly (113:7; see Zeph 3:12).
verses.3: "when they are sick:" This illness might be physical or spiritual (see 6:2; Ps 38).
verses.4: The psalmist applies the blessing to himself (41:12). Apparently he has taken care of the poor (41:1), but he has sinned against the Lord in other ways. Out of his pain, he cries for healing while confessing his sin. The Lord alone can grant the restoration that brings true joy (30:2; 107:20-21).
verses.5: "How soon will he die?" The psalmist’s opponents regard his suffering as a divine judgment (cp. 1:6).
verses.9: "the one who shared my food:" Eating together was a sign of unity (Acts 2:42). Refusing to eat with someone indicated hostility (1 Cor 5:11). Jesus experienced the same kind of betrayal (John 13:1, 18).
verses.13: This doxology closes Book One (Pss 1–41). Cp. 106:48.
verses.1-13: In this wisdom psalm, the psalmist prays for healing (41:4, 10), laments his distress (41:5-9), and expresses confidence in the Lord’s blessing (41:1-3, 11-12).
verses.5-9: The psalmist’s enemies disguise themselves as friends, while his friends openly become his enemies.
verses.11-12: The psalmist knows that the Lord has forgiven him and will bless him.

verses.1: title "The descendants of Korah" were members of a Levitical choir appointed by David to serve as Temple singers (see 1 Chr 6:22-38; 9:19-34; 2 Chr 20:19). Their ancestor Korah was the apostate who had rebelled against Moses and whom the earth swallowed up (Exod 6:24; Num 16).
verses.3: Having "tears for food" speaks of great grief (80:5; 102:9; see 6:6; 56:8; 119:136; 126:5). • The wicked try to hold God to their timetable and deny his power to intervene.
verses.4: The psalmist recalls "leading a great procession" as a member of the Levitical choir, possibly during the high holy days.
verses.5: The psalmist feels depressed, but it does not incapacitate him. He remembers that the living God is his "Savior". This verse is repeated in 42:11 and 43:5.
verses.6: "Mount Hermon" is a high mountain range northeast of Israel. The "source of the Jordan" is by Dan at the foot of Mount Hermon. • "Mount Mizar" might be a peak in the Mount Hermon range.
verses.7: The "raging seas", "waves", and "surging tides" conjure images of God’s wrath (see 88:7).
verses.8: The psalmist sees rays of hope. A life oriented to God includes "songs" of joy and "praying" for justice and vindication (42:9-10; 43:1-4).
verses.1-5: These psalms, like Pss 9 and 10, form a unit comprising a lament with a bittersweet refrain of hope (42:5, 11; 43:5). In many Hebrew manuscripts these two psalms are combined as one. The historical context is uncertain; these psalms might be the voice of God’s people in exile, confessing their loyalty to God as he punishes them for their prevailing apostasy. The psalmist longs for fellowship with God such as he enjoyed in Jerusalem (42:4); his memories only make him more discouraged. As the psalmist cries out to God, he recalls God’s love and faithfulness (42:8), which moves him to plead for vindication (43:1-4).
verses.1-4: The psalmist’s longing for God comes from being geographically distant from the Temple as he remembers the past. • The verb translated "longs" is found only here and in Joel 1:20 (“cry out”); in both cases it refers to extreme "thirst" in a waterless desert (see Pss 63:1; 143:6; see also 84:2).
verses.5-6: The psalmist encourages himself with questions and answers.
verses.9-10: The psalmist brings his many doubts, discouragements, and questions directly to God.

verses.2: "tossed me aside:" Other psalms similarly ask whether God has rejected his people (44:9, 23; 60:1, 10; 74:1; 77:7; 88:14; 89:38; 108:11).
verses.3: In this prayer for God’s redemption, "light" and "truth" are viewed as guides (see 18:25-29; 27:1; 85:10-13; 89:14-18; see also 119:105; John 3:19; Eph 5:8; 1 Thes 5:5-7). • The Temple on the "mountain" in Jerusalem symbolized God’s "holy" presence among his people (Pss 15:1; 43:3; 99:5, 9; 132:7).
verses.5: This verse is repeated in 42:5, 11.
verses.1-4: The psalmist turns to the Lord for rescue from his troubles, for guidance, for restoration, and for vindication.

verses.1: "we have heard . . . of all you did:" The story of redemption encompasses the story of God’s favor and power in his past acts of rescue (see 78:1-4; see also Pss 105–106).
verses.2: God "drove out the pagan nations" during the conquests recorded in Joshua.
verses.3: Though the Israelites used "swords" and other weapons (44:6), they would have lost their battles without the "light" of the Lord’s favor (see 18:25-29; 27:1; 89:15).
verses.11: "scattered us among the nations:" This probably refers to the Exile (see 51:18-19; 89:38-51; 106:40-47; 137).
verses.22: Paul quotes this verse as a parenthetical aside in his list of things that cannot separate us from Christ’s love (Rom 8:36).
verses.23: "Wake up:" Biblical authors often call for God’s attention in a crisis (35:23; 44:23; 73:20; 80:2; Mark 4:38).
verses.1-26: This national lament after defeat in battle continues the tone of the previous two psalms, including reflecting on an unspecified moment in Israel’s history and calling on God for salvation. The people recite God’s past acts of rescue (44:1-3), acknowledge God’s power to save (44:4-8), describe their humiliation in exile (44:9-16), claim their innocence and lament the injustice of their current situation (44:17-22), and cry for vindication (44:23-26).
verses.4-8: God’s people feel confident about his mighty acts; he was with them in the past, and he is their king in the present.
verses.9-16: The people have experienced defeat (44:9-12), so they understand suffering and disgrace (44:13-16).
verses.23-26: In the end, God’s people can turn to the Lord and trust him for rescue. Their petition for God to remedy their situation is as strong as their lament about God’s rejection.

verses.1: title The "tune “Lilies”" is no longer known (see also Ps 69).
verses.2: This general description of the king’s symbolic status anticipates his permanent legacy (45:16). That the Lord has "blessed" him and charged him to bear God’s attributes is symbolized by his "handsome" appearance and "gracious words".
verses.3: Glory and majesty belong to the Lord (96:6; 111:3).
verses.4: As God’s agent of "truth, humility, and justice" (see 72:1-2, 4, 7), the king can carry out "awe-inspiring deeds" (65:5; 96:4).
verses.6: "Justice" characterizes God’s "rule", as it should characterize the king’s administration.
verses.8: Fine spices mixed with oil create distinctive perfumes. • The king’s "palaces" were wood paneled with ivory inlays (cp. 6:4; Amos 3:15).
verses.9: Marriages often sealed diplomatic connections between kings; the "women" became part of the harem (see 1 Kgs 11:1-3).
verses.12: "The princess of Tyre:" Israel traded with Tyre, a powerful city-state. The noblest woman of the city bears a wedding gift to her counterpart, the new queen, who represents an honored kingdom.
verses.1-17: This psalm celebrates a royal wedding; it might have been sung on many occasions and not just at one wedding. As God’s representative, the king carried the responsibility of dispensing justice and maintaining order in God’s world (see Ps 2).
verses.3-5: The psalmist expounds on the royal splendor the king showed when fighting his enemies.
verses.6-9: The king is like a god among humans; he is anointed by God, he has received a mighty throne, and he dispenses justice as he rules forever. • The writer to the Hebrews applies 45:6-7 to Jesus as he argues that the Son is greater than the angels (Heb 1:8-9).
verses.10-12: The bride is a representative of the king. Powerful people and nations try to gain her favor in order to get close to the king. This is a great honor, and she is encouraged to give herself fully to her new position.

verses.1: title "sung by soprano voices:" Hebrew according to alamoth (“maidens”; see also study note on 1 Chr 15:20). In worship, a choir or a group of instrumentalists performed this hymn.
verses.4: Like the streams flowing through Eden, this "river" brings the water of life, restoration, and healing (36:8-9; see Gen 2:10; Ezek 47; Rev 22:2).
verses.5: "From the very break of day:" In the ancient Near East, enemies attacked cities during the day; even during the most dangerous times, the Lord "will protect" the place where his name dwells.
verses.6: People and "nations" live "in chaos", characterized by opportunism (83:2), busyness (39:6), and noise. These people shake, totter, and "crumble", unlike the city of God (cp. 15:5). In contrast, when the godly feel disturbed, they cry out for God’s help (42:5, 11; 43:5; 55:17).
verses.7: This refrain reminds readers of the identity of the God of Zion. • "among us:" Hebrew ‘immanu, part of the name Immanuel, “God with us” (Isa 7:14; 8:8; Matt 1:23).
verses.8: Israel saw the Lord’s "glorious works" in the wilderness (107:24; 111:2), but the wicked, who have no concern for them (28:5), are left desolate (73:19).
verses.10: A message directly from the Lord confirms the authenticity of the psalmist’s vision (see also 12:5-6; 32:8). • "know that I am God:" The Lord will do what he promises (Isa 45:3; 49:23; 60:16). • God will be exalted (Ps 47; Isa 6:1); he will judge the nations and rescue his people (see Pss 57:11; 89:13; 108:5-6; 118:16).
verses.1-11: This psalm of Zion celebrates God’s special presence in Jerusalem (see also Pss 48, 76, 87, 122), inviting confidence in the Lord because the citizens of Zion enjoy his protection.
verses.1-3: Even when faced with natural disasters, the citizens of Zion express no fear.
verses.4-6: The strong city where "God dwells" protects its inhabitants. They enjoy the "river" flowing inside the city. This river contrasts with the turbulent waters (the powers of the nations) outside the city.
verses.8-9: This invitation to trust in the Lord offers a perspective on God’s interactions with human powers.

verses.1: People "clap" their "hands" in praise and recognition of marvelous deeds (47:3-4; see 98:8; Isa 55:12; cp. Nah 3:19).
verses.4: "Jacob’s descendants:" Jacob was the father of all Israelites (Gen 32:28); the name Jacob often represents the nation of Israel. • God "loves" and commits himself to Jacob (see Pss 78:68; 127:2; see Rom 11:28).
verses.5: "trumpets:" Or rams’ horns (see 81:3). At times, rams’ horns were sounded in celebration (98:5-6; 2 Kgs 11:14; 1 Chr 15:28).
verses.7: People from "all the earth" (see 96:1-3) will worship God.
verses.1-9: This psalm celebrates God’s kingship over all the earth; it tells of God’s victory in dealing with Israel and the nations. Both Israel (47:3-4) and the nations (47:9) participate in God’s kingdom.
verses.1-2: As the sovereign king over the nations, God requires praise.
verses.3-4: The Lord made Israel victorious, especially under David (see 18:40-50). God’s mighty deeds of redemption manifest his love for Israel.
verses.5-6: The psalmist portrays the Lord as returning to heaven, having accomplished his victories. For a portrayal of his descent, see 18:9-16.

verses.3: God dwells in Zion to protect it from all enemies (see 46:5).
verses.7: The "ships of Tarshish", built for long voyages, represent human accomplishment (see also 2 Chr 9:21; Isa 2:16). Their destruction might be the event mentioned in 1 Kgs 22:48.
verses.14: No one is like God (35:10; 71:19; 86:8; 89:6, 8; 113:5; see Isa 40:18, 25). He is the shepherd King (Ps 95:7) who "will guide" (see 5:8; 23:2) the sheep of his flock (77:20).
verses.1-14: This song of Zion (see also Pss 46, 76, 87, 122) explicitly views Jerusalem (Zion) as the city of the Great King where the godly find protection (48:1-3). God rules from Zion in faithfulness, righteousness, and justice, and he inspires his subjects with confidence and joy (48:9-11). They commit themselves to seeing the glory of Zion for themselves so that they can tell the next generation about it (48:8, 12-14).
verses.9-11: The psalmist joyfully celebrates the Lord’s presence in the midst of the community, reflecting on the faithfulness, righteousness, and justice of God’s rule.
verses.12-13: "towers . . . fortified walls . . . citadels:" These structures provide a visual tour of Zion’s strength.

verses.4: The teacher used both "proverbs" and "riddles" for instruction in wisdom (see Prov 1:5-6).
verses.1-20: In this wisdom psalm, a wise teacher warns against enemies, whom he portrays as living a rich lifestyle and caring only for themselves (49:5-9). They cannot keep anyone alive, least of all themselves, even in their memories (49:10-12). Like fattened animals, they are led to slaughter (49:14-20).
verses.1-4: The wisdom teacher invites everyone to the hall of wisdom; he promises to instruct with a proverb and a riddle.
verses.1-2: Anyone who will "listen" can gain wisdom (Prov 1:5, 8, 33).
verses.5-8: If enemies who live for material rewards cannot sustain themselves, how can they give life to others?
verses.11-12: The teacher brings wisdom through irony. Everyone dies, and even those with "estates" named after them will be forgotten.
verses.13-15: The teachers of false wisdom cannot rescue themselves from death. Only God has that power.
verses.16-20: The "wicked" might have rich, luxurious lives, but they forget that they cannot avoid death.

verses.9: Unlike pagan gods, God does "not need" food; instead, he wants his people to serve him with a right heart (50:14-15).
verses.10: "I own the cattle on a thousand hills:" God has no needs; he possesses everything.
verses.14: "Thankfulness" means looking beyond self-interest to express gratitude for God’s blessings (see 51:15-17; 54:6). • True "sacrifice" requires offering one’s self to the glory of God (50:23; Rom 12:1-2).
verses.15: God’s response to his people’s cry is to "rescue" them.
verses.17: "my discipline . . . my words:" The wicked may observe rituals, but they reject more important matters such as justice, mercy, and faithfulness (cp. Matt 23:23-24).
verses.21: Because he is patient, God "remained silent".
verses.22: God "will tear" the wicked "apart" like a lion tearing its prey (Isa 5:29; 31:4; Ezek 19:3; cp. Pss 7:2; 22:13).
verses.1-23: God appears as judge to remind the godly and the ungodly in turn that outward performance of sacrificial rituals and recitation of the law are worthless without thankfulness, repentance, and justice.
verses.1-3: The whole universe must pay attention when "God approaches" to bring justice into the world.
verses.4-6: The Lord is coming to bring righteousness. This hope encourages his "faithful people", but those who have been unfaithful will not experience blessing when "the heavens above and earth below" testify against them (cp. Deut 30:19; 31:28; 32:1; Isa 1:2). The Lord comes to restore order to the world (Pss 5:8; 22:31; 33:5; 40:9; 50:6; 71:16; 97:6).
verses.7-13: The psalmist delivers a message against those who regard the sacrificial rituals as more important than having a proper heart attitude.
verses.16-21: This message is against the wicked, who only pretend to listen to God.
verses.22-23: The wicked will experience God’s justice, while the godly will see God’s everlasting salvation.

verses.1: A prayer for God’s "mercy" and kindness is part of the genre of lament. Sometimes the plea comes from the psalmist’s acknowledgment of his weakness and sin, as here (see also 6:2; 9:13; 25:16; 31:9; 41:4, 10). At other times, it arises from the psalmist’s commitment to the Lord (see 26:11; 27:7; 119:29, 58, 132). In each case, God’s mercy brings an inner renewal.
verses.2: "Wash me . . . Purify me:" The psalmist prays for cleansing and release from the "guilt" of his sin (51:7; see 26:6; Isa 1:16, 18; 4:4).
verses.4: "Against . . . you alone:" This is hyperbole—the psalmist knows he also "sinned" against human beings (2 Sam 11:2-4, 15-17), but his offense against God is more important. He expects God to rebuke him and will accept whatever verdict God renders (see Rom 3:4).
verses.5: "I was born a sinner:" The psalmist is not making excuses but is acknowledging the depth of his sinfulness. From the time we are "conceived", we all share in the human condition of sinfulness.
verses.7: "Purify me from my sins" (literally Purify me with the hyssop branch; see Exod 12:22; Lev 14:4; John 19:29; Heb 9:19): The psalmist depends on God to purify and renew him (see Isa 1:18).
verses.8: Regaining "joy" is a gracious gift from God. • "you have broken me:" The psalmist’s whole being feels broken (6:2; cp. 34:20).
verses.10: "A loyal spirit" yields the inner qualities of constancy and perseverance.
verses.11: "your Holy Spirit:" Only the power of the Holy Spirit can change the human will to make it “loyal” (51:10) and “willing to obey” (51:12).
verses.13: As he learns from his sin and its consequences, the psalmist wants to "teach" others.
verses.14: "shedding blood:" This idiom includes any injustice, not just homicide (9:12; 58:10; see 2 Sam 11:14-26; cp. Isa 1:15-17).
verses.19: "Sacrifices offered in the right spirit" come from a heart that is right with God and with others (see 15:2-5; 24:3-6; 50:14; Matt 5:23-24).
verses.1-13: These psalms of David share a common thread in their reflection on the experience of evil. In Ps 51, the psalmist confesses the evil he has done and asks God’s forgiveness. Psalms 52–64 lament specific evils that David experienced. A song of praise (Ps 65) brings David’s laments to an end.
verses.1-19: This moving prayer for restoration asks for God’s favor, mercy, forgiveness, and cleansing. Out of a broken spirit, the psalmist confesses and accepts responsibility for his sin (51:3-6), then petitions God to remove his guilt and renew him inwardly (51:7-12). The psalmist then recommits himself to a lifestyle of wisdom and joy in the service of God and others (51:13-17).
verses.1-2: The repentant offender has nothing to offer God. He needs God’s favor, mercy, forgiveness, and blessing before he can experience renewal and restoration.
verses.3-6: The psalmist accepts the consequences of his sin against God. He knows that there is nothing good in him unless God renews his life.
verses.10-12: God’s Spirit renews and recreates the human spirit.
verses.18-19: "rebuild the walls of Jerusalem:" These verses were probably added as a prayer for national restoration after the Exile (see Pss 42–43); the entire community in exile identified with the spirit of the psalm.

verses.1: title This psalm refers to an incident in 1 Sam 21:1-10; 22:9-10. The accuser, "Doeg the Edomite", is a paradigm of evil.
verses.3: Deceptive speech changes one’s character.
verses.5: God "will strike" the wicked "down "like a pagan altar, idol, or unclean vessel (Exod 34:13; Lev 11:35; 2 Kgs 10:27).
verses.6: In Hebrew, the verbs here translated "see" and "be amazed" sound almost alike.
verses.1-9: Wicked people use words to destroy relationships and communities. They foolishly think that they can be heroes by their words (52:1-4), but their fate suddenly overtakes them (52:5-7). In contrast, the godly renew their commitment to the Lord (52:8-9) and find their future secure in him.
verses.1-4: Liars foolishly deceive themselves by thinking that they can be heroes by their words. They believe themselves innocent of any charges of evildoing, though they love evil and cause destruction. Those who speak curses, sarcasm, bitterness, arrogant boasting, and deceptions (31:18; 34:13; 59:7, 12; 120:2-3; 140:3, 9) bring about chaos, alienation, and destruction (Jas 3:5). Their sharp words cut like swords and daggers (Pss 55:21; 57:4; 64:3), the fangs of a snake (140:3), or a "razor."
verses.5-7: God’s judgment on the wicked will come suddenly and forcibly. The godly rejoice in God’s justice, not in the misfortunes of the wicked.
verses.8-9: The psalmist commits himself to a life of trust in the Lord. • An "olive tree" lives a long time when cared for (1:3; 128:3). The psalmist desires to be close to the Lord, his Savior and the source of his blessing (18:6; 23:6).

verses.5: "scatter the bones:" Israel’s "enemies" would suffer shameful defeat and lack the peaceful rest of a decent burial (cp. 141:7; 2 Kgs 9:10; Jer 8:1-2; Ezek 6:5).
verses.1-6: This psalm parallels Ps 14, differing only in verse 5.
verses.1-3: Paul uses the Greek translation of this passage in his description of the depravity of all people (Rom 3:10-12).

verses.1: title This psalm refers to the account of 1 Sam 23:19-20, when the "Ziphites" were bent on violence.
verses.3: The "strangers" were alienated from the covenant community (see 109:11; Prov 5:10). • Proud and "violent people" hold no regard for God or for other people (see Pss 35:11, 25; 86:14; Prov 11:16).
verses.6: A "voluntary offering" is a sacrifice of praise. Sacrifices of praise are the kind of offering God most desires (see Ps 50:14-15, 23).
verses.1-7: In this individual lament, occasioned by violent and godless people (54:3), the psalmist turns to God in prayer and maintains his focus on God’s help (54:4). He prays for God to save him from evil and to judge his enemies (54:5, 7).
verses.6-7: In anticipation of God’s response, the mood of the psalm changes from gloom to thanksgiving.

verses.23: To "die young" means that one fails to experience God’s full blessing (cp. Prov 3:2, 16).
verses.1-23: The psalmist is faced with adversaries whose leader is a former friend (55:12-14), and he is overwhelmed with anguish. He turns to the Lord in prayer and commits himself to the Lord for redress (55:22-23). Jesus experienced similar suffering when his friend (Judas) betrayed him. He also experienced the answer to the psalmist’s prayer: (1) by taking the place of the wicked and receiving their judgment (Isa 53:7-9), and (2) by committing himself to the Father, who rescued (Luke 23:46) and rewarded him (Isa 53:10-12).
verses.1-3: The occasion for this prayer is an attack by an enemy.
verses.4-8: In the experience of deep anguish, the psalmist confesses that his adversity has become unbearable and he seeks an escape.
verses.12-20: The psalmist’s enemy was once a "friend"; memories of that close relationship bring him pain (see 31:11).
verses.19-21: God is good and faithful, but the psalmist’s enemies and so-called friend are deceitful and wicked.
verses.22-23: The psalmist commits all his cares "to the" Lord.

verses.1: title David was "seized" by "Philistines" concerned about his loyalties and brought before King Achish (1 Sam 21:10-15).
verses.4: "mere mortals:" Or mere flesh, in contrast to the immortal and infinitely more powerful God (see Isa 2:22).
verses.8: The psalmist makes a play on the Hebrew words translated "sorrows" (Hebrew nod) and "bottle" (Hebrew no’d).
verses.11: "mere mortals" (Hebrew ’adam)":" The psalm also uses two other words for man: ’enosh (“people,” 56:1) and basar (“mere mortals,” 56:4). All express the ideas of mortality and finitude.
verses.13: The "light" of God’s goodness and salvation will replace the darkness of "death" (see 18:25-29; 27:1).
verses.1-13: This individual lament moves from petition to confidence two times (56:1-4, 5-13).
verses.5-7: The psalmist specifies his charge against his attackers as he prays for their evil to cease.

verses.1: "shadow of your wings:" As a bird protects its young, God protects the one who trusts in him (see 17:8).
verses.2: "God Most High" (Hebrew Elohim-Elyon) is a generic title for God, who is more powerful than all real or imagined supernatural beings (see 91:1; 97:9; Gen 14:18-22). • "who will fulfill his purpose:" Or who will end my [trouble], or who deals kindly with me.
verses.5: This verse is repeated in 57:11 and 108:5. • God’s "glory"—his manifest presence that excludes all evil (8:1; 19:1-4; 24:7)—will fill the whole created order (Isa 6:3).
verses.1-11: The psalmist’s cry for mercy and protection quickly turns into an affirmation of trust and confidence in the Lord (57:1-4). When the wicked fall into their own traps (57:6), the psalmist will praise the Lord (57:7-10).
verses.3-4: These verses are a prayer for rescue from powerful enemies. The metaphor of "fierce lions" describes human enemies; the psalmist feels unable to escape them without God’s intervention (see also 35:11-21; 124:6).
verses.7-11: This section is repeated with a few modifications in 108:1-5.
verses.7-8: The psalmist is "confident" that God will end the night of evil (cp. 56:13).
verses.10-11: God’s glory extends to the whole universe, as will praise for his "unfailing love" and "faithfulness".

verses.1: "rulers" (or gods): This designation was used for high officials and administrators of "justice" (82:1, 6). Elsewhere, it might refer to angelic creatures (89:7) or to the gods of the nations (82:1; Dan 11:36).
verses.3: All human beings are "born sinners" (see 51:5); however, whereas the "wicked" indulge their sinful nature, the godly fight against it (Rom 7:19-23; Jas 4:1-10).
verses.4: "Venom" here means poisonous speech (see 140:3).
verses.6: The psalmist calls on God to "break" the destructive power of the wicked.
verses.8: When moving over dry ground, "snails" dry up.
verses.11: Vindication is the reward of "those who live for God".
verses.1-11: The administration of justice is a mark of good government. God expects nothing less from his people. The psalmist condemns Israel’s leaders for abusing their power, and he calls on the Lord to rain down his curses upon the wicked. The demonstration of divine justice will reassure the godly that God is just.
verses.1-5: The administrators of justice were furthering their own interests rather than those of the needy. The absence of justice gradually resulted in a violent society.
verses.9-10: God’s judgment will come suddenly. The certainty of vindication brings joy to the godly.

verses.1: title "the time Saul sent soldiers to watch David’s house:" See 1 Sam 19:11-18.
verses.1-17: The psalmist laments the power of enemies who conspire with other nations.
verses.1-2: "Protect me" (or place me on high): When surrounded by evil, the godly pray for God to set them apart for himself and protect them.
verses.4-5: The psalmist asks God to show the treacherous, deceptive, and "wicked traitors" no mercy (see 25:2).
verses.6-8: The wicked threaten like "vicious dogs", but the Lord responds with scorn.
verses.11-13: The psalmist prays that the wicked will be forced to endure the same agonizing pain they have caused.
verses.14-16: The wicked will go "unsatisfied", but the psalmist will praise the Lord’s "power" and "unfailing love".

verses.1: title "useful for teaching:" This psalm was taught to young people as part of their education. • "regarding the time:" See 2 Sam 8:13-14. • "Aram-naharaim" and "Aram-zobah" refer to the Arameans of northwest Mesopotamia and Syria (see study note on Gen 24:10). • The "tune “Lily of the Testimony”" is unknown today.
verses.3: "wine" (Hebrew yayin) "that sent us reeling:" Yayin, the generic Hebrew term meaning “wine,” is often associated with drunkenness (2 Sam 13:28; Isa 5:11; 28:7-8; cp. Ps 104:15; Deut 14:26; Isa 55:1); it symbolized God’s judgment of the wicked (Ps 75:8; Jer 51:7).
verses.4: God "raised a banner" over his people to serve as "a rallying point" and as a source of pride and confidence. • The "fear" of God that leads to wisdom (111:10) is not weakness; it provides the perspective and strength required to do what is right.
verses.5: The psalmist prays for rescue based on the special relationship between God and his people.
verses.6: "Shechem" and "Succoth" represent Israel’s heartland.
verses.9: Destroying a defeated invader’s capital ("the fortified city") would help to ensure that they would not attack again. The capital of "Edom" was Bozrah, located to the southeast of Israel. Only God could grant "victory."
verses.1-12: The psalmist laments a national defeat and cries out to God for rescue.
verses.1-4: When God’s people experience his discipline, they affirm their loyalty and await God’s answer.
verses.5-12: This section is repeated verbatim in 108:6-13.
verses.6-8: The Lord responds with a message of promise. He shares his land with his people as spoils of war.

verses.2: "the ends of the earth:" This expression has the connotation of a cry that comes from a place far away from God. • The psalmist’s "heart is overwhelmed" with deep anguish.
verses.4: The poet longs for God’s presence and seeks entrance into God’s home on earth for divine protection and care. To be received into God’s "sanctuary" (literally tent) is the greatest good (see 15:1; 23:6; 24:3-6). The Hebrew word translated sanctuary recalls the Tabernacle and the tent that David built for the Ark (1 Chr 15:1). See also study note on John 1:14. • The "shelter of your wings" symbolizes God’s protection and care (see Pss 9:9; 17:8).
verses.5: "you have heard my vows:" The psalmist’s vows might also be a part of ceremonial sacrifices (66:13-15; 76:11; 116:14, 18). He praises and thanks God for his rescue. • The "inheritance" refers to the promise of the land (see Ps 60), the sacredness of the Temple, the joy of God’s presence (119:111), or any similar reward (16:6; 37:9, 11, 18, 22, 29, 34; 127:3).
verses.1-11: In these royal prayers, the psalmist longs for God’s presence. All three psalms concern themselves with the king’s security.
verses.1-8: The lamenting psalmist petitions God to protect him and lead him into his presence (61:4-5). He prays for God to extend and protect the king’s rule and makes vows to praise God.

verses.1: title "Jeduthun:" See 1 Chr 25:1; also in Pss 39 and 77.
verses.4: "My high position" refers to the royal throne.
verses.9: "not what they appear to be:" People often try to look stronger and better than they are.
verses.10: The crime of "extortion" means using intimidation and threats to make others give up what is theirs, while "stealing" is taking what belongs to others.
verses.1-12: This psalm expresses confidence in the king and offers prayer for him. The king rests in God despite his difficulties. Although his deceptive and powerful adversaries push hard against him, he remains undaunted. He encourages himself and his people to trust in God and to see their human adversaries from God’s perspective, where they appear frail, fleeting, and deceptive (62:9).
verses.3-4: The enemies desire to topple the king with lies and cunning.
verses.5-8: The psalmist encourages himself and others to place their hope in God.
verses.9-12: Unlike God, humans are transient beings. Even when they thrive, their prosperity is fleeting.
verses.11-12: Strength and "unfailing love" remain in balance only in God. He cares for his people by ridding the world of evildoers (see 1:6).

verses.1: Together, "soul" and "whole body" refer to a person’s entire being. • "parched and weary land:" When David was living in the desert, he also found himself in a spiritual wasteland, separated from God’s people and the sanctuary.
verses.2: The psalmist remembers that he had found God to be present in his "sanctuary" (see 18:6; 61:4; 62:5, 11-12).
verses.3: "better than life itself:" The highest quality of life is found in relationship with God (see 4:7; 63:5; Prov 16:8).
verses.6: "Meditating" on God requires focused awareness, concentration, thought, and reflection (see 1:2).
verses.9: The wicked were "plotting to destroy" the psalmist’s life through deception and lies, but they would meet their end. • The "depths of the earth" refers to the place of the dead.
verses.10: Wild "jackals" are associated with desolation and abandonment (Isa 13:20-22; 34:10-15; Jer 9:11; 49:33; 51:37; Lam 5:18; Mal 1:3). The wicked will not receive honor in death; their bodies will be left to scavenging animals (Eccl 6:3; Jer 22:18-19; 36:29-30).
verses.1-11: The king longs for God’s presence so vividly that he eats, drinks, and sees God’s goodness. Though worn out and harassed by the wicked, the king sees God, and this animates him with praise. God becomes his life (63:3), while the wicked perish (63:9).
verses.6-8: The psalmist reflects and meditates on God’s presence "through the night". In the absence of light, God is the light. The quietness of the night and the longing for dawn provide time to focus on the true significance of life with the Lord.

verses.3: "their tongues . . . bitter words:" Liars use their speech to kill. This description might also refer to practicing magic.
verses.6: The enemies create a "perfect plan" to harm the innocent without getting caught. • Human beings will sink to unthinkable depths with evil words, acts, or plans (83:3; see Jer 17:9).
verses.1-10: This lament decries the destructive plots and arrogant attitude of the wicked (64:1-6). The psalmist turns to God in prayer and takes heart in God’s justice because whatever the wicked do will be undone by the righteous judge. The godly will rejoice and grow in wisdom as they reflect on God’s mighty acts.
verses.1-6: These verses form a prayer for rescue from bold and powerful liars.
verses.7-10: What God does is righteous. God undoes what is wicked and pays the wicked back with what they planned for others.

verses.1: God alone deserves "praise" and is worthy to have "vows" made to him.
verses.2: "All of us" means all humans.
verses.3: "you forgive:" God graciously removes the guilt of sin (see 32:5).
verses.4: "those you choose to bring near:" This includes people from Israel and from other nations. • Only those whom God sees as blameless "live in" his "holy courts" (Pss 15 and 24). • At the "Temple", God’s earthly palace, all nations can gather to experience God’s holy presence. No structure can separate humans from God (see Rev 21:22).
verses.8: All over the world (Job 38:13; see Ps 50:1-3), people should "stand in awe of" the Lord.
verses.9: The "river of God" and all rivers demonstrate God’s victorious power and goodness through the order in nature and the regularity of the harvests (see 1:3; 36:8; 46:4; Ezek 47:6-12; Zech 14:8; Rev 22:1).
verses.13: Nature bursts out in praise of the Creator (see 79:13; 96:11-13; 148:3-5, 7-12; Isa 55:12-13).
verses.1-13: This psalm recounts the reasons why all people should praise and revere God for his almighty power and merciful care for his universe.
verses.1-3: Praise is the appropriate response to God’s majestic deeds in redemption (65:3-5) and in nature (65:5-13).
verses.6-7: God brought order to "the mountains", the "raging oceans", and the "pounding waves" (see Pss 95:4-5; 104:6-9). • The psalmist compares the chaotic forces of nature with the rebellion of the "nations" (see 2:1-12; 33:6-11; 46:6).
verses.9-13: The created order provides clear evidence of God’s power (65:6-8). He shows his love by maintaining nature. Everything praises the Lord as all the parts fit together harmoniously.

verses.2: The "glory of his name" represents the perfection of God’s character.
verses.3: God conquers his "enemies" (see 18:44; 59:11; 81:15).
verses.7: God’s "power" brings redemption. The same word occurs in 65:6 for God’s power in creation (see also 80:2).
verses.9: God guides his people into wisdom and away from folly (17:5; 37:31; 121:3).
verses.10: "You have tested us, O God:" As the silversmith heats "silver" to remove the dross, God’s discipline removes sin from his people (see 12:6).
verses.11: God decrees and permits the many trying circumstances his people experience.
verses.12: "Then you put a leader over us:" Or You made people ride over our heads. This expression possibly refers to a foreign ruler who kept the Israelites in submission.
verses.15: Vows often included sacrifices of thanksgiving, including "burnt offerings" (see 20:3; 40:6; 50:8; 51:19).
verses.1-20: This anonymous psalm includes two hymns (66:1-12, 13-20) that praise God for his redemption.
verses.1-4: The psalmist exhorts nature to join in a mighty chorus to praise God’s glory, name, and power.
verses.5-7: The story of the Exodus and God’s victory over the sea evokes responses of astonishment (66:5) and worship (66:6). God works "miracles . . . for people" in order to redeem them for himself.
verses.8-10: The orderly lives of the redeemed reflect the order of God’s world. The Lord protects them from evil and purifies them.
verses.16-20: The private testimony in the conclusion of the psalm parallels the public praise of its opening (66:1-4).

verses.3: God’s international reputation leads to his praise among the "nations" (see 138:4), whose turmoil and rebelliousness will cease when they join Israel in praise of God. • One God rules over all, and the nations will give thanks for God’s just rule (see 67:4).
verses.4: God brings the ultimate "justice" that human beings desire (96:10; 98:9).
verses.1-7: In this anonymous prayer for God’s blessing, the psalmist addresses the knowledge and worship of God among the nations (cp. 64:9; 65:8). The prayer requests that God’s name be kept holy and that his kingdom come (cp. Matt 6:9-13).
verses.1-2: This prayer is based on the priestly blessing found in Num 6:24-26. God’s goodness to Israel affects his reputation among the nations (see Ps 96:1-3).
verses.6-7: Bountiful "harvests" are evidence of God’s blessing (Gen 26:12; Isa 30:23). • "all over the world:" See Pss 2:8; 96:1-3. • All "will fear him", joining with Israel to acknowledge the God of Israel.

verses.2: Both "smoke" and "wax" represent a transitory existence (22:12-18; 37:20; 102:3).
verses.3: The lot of "the godly" contrasts with that of the wicked (see 1:6).
verses.4: "him who rides the clouds:" This is an ancient description of Baal, a Canaanite deity. The psalmist applies it to "the" Lord as the true “Rider of the Clouds” (see 68:33; 104:3). God wields power over the clouds and the rain.
verses.5: God, the "Father" of all marginalized and needy people, shows them compassion and protects their rights (see 10:14, 18; 69:33; 82:3). • Like his "dwelling", the Lord "is holy". The supreme example of the holy God coming down to rescue humanity is Jesus Christ.
verses.6: God released Israel from slavery in Egypt (Exod 20:2; see Ps 69:33), and he still "sets the prisoners free". • The "sun-scorched" desert represents alienation from God and separation from blessing.
verses.11: "a great army" (or a host of women)" brings:" The Hebrew suggests women singers caroling "the good news" of victory (see 68:25; Exod 15:20).
verses.13: The seminomadic pastoral people "who lived among the sheepfolds" were surprised to receive "silver" and "gold" carvings from the battle.
verses.14: "The Almighty" (Hebrew Shaddai) is an ancient designation for God (see 91:1; Gen 17:1). • The identification of "Mount Zalmon" is uncertain; it was possibly a mountain in Bashan (see Ps 68:15).
verses.15: "Bashan" is a plateau northeast of Jerusalem and east of the Sea of Galilee that was known for its woods and pastureland (see 22:12; Isa 2:13). The "mountains" might have included Mount Hermon to the north of the plateau or Mount Zalmon, which might be Jebel ed-Druze on the east.
verses.16: "Why do you look with envy?" Bashan is physically much more impressive than the mountains around Jerusalem, but it was not the home of the Lord. Only Mount Zion enjoyed the privilege of providing God’s dwelling place.
verses.17: "Chariots", the ultimate weapon of the armed forces in the psalmist’s day, are an image of the Lord’s power to grant victory (20:7; 44:3).
verses.18: "When you ascended to the heights:" The Most High established his reign victoriously in Zion. • "a crowd of captives . . . gifts:" This is an image of a victorious ruler leading the victory march after battle. Paul applied this image to Jesus Christ (Eph 4:8-13).
verses.19: Like a caring father or a shepherd, God "carries" his people "in his arms" (see 55:22; 68:5-6).
verses.21: "God will smash the heads of his enemies:" Cp. Gen 3:15.
verses.22: God will deal with all "enemies", whether from high places (represented by "Bashan") or low ("the depths of the sea").
verses.29: The conquered "kings" will bring gifts to the Lord.
verses.30: Hostile and rebellious people delight in warfare and insurrection (see 2:1-3).
verses.32: The term "kingdoms of the earth" includes all nations and power structures.
verses.34: When the Lord demonstrates his "power"," majesty", and "strength" against the nations, he strengthens his people (see 96:4-6).
verses.1-35: This prayer for God’s victorious rule traces God’s march from Sinai to Zion (68:7, 16-18, 24). He rescued the nation of Israel from Egypt, guided it through the wilderness, brought it into the Promised Land, and established his kingdom. He is a caring and victorious God, whose nature is unchanging. Therefore, the godly hope and rejoice in the prospect of God’s universal dominion.
verses.1-3: These verses form a prayer for God to "rise up" and "scatter" his "enemies", as he did when Israel entered the Promised Land (cp. Num 10:35-36; Josh 6–12).
verses.4-6: The psalmist praises God’s powerful and compassionate reign.
verses.8-10: The "earth trembled" as in an earthquake (see Exod 19:18). • "the heavens poured down rain:" Wells in the desert and rain showers in Canaan supplied an abundance of water.
verses.19-20: The Divine Warrior cares for his people like a shepherd; the people praise him.
verses.24-27: A great company joins together in the pilgrimage to Zion.
verses.28-31: The people pray for God’s success and for victory over the enemy nations (68:1-3).
verses.32-35: The psalmist calls for the people to praise God, who is victorious over his enemies.

verses.1: title "to the tune “Lilies”:" Psalm 45 also notes this tune, but Ps 45 celebrates the glory of kingship, whereas Ps 69 is the cry of a tired king who feels abandoned by the Lord.
verses.4: John applied this lament to Jesus (John 15:25).
verses.9: Though the psalmist concerns himself with God and all that is holy, "insults" have been his earthly reward. This verse was later applied to Jesus’ anger at the Temple’s money changers (John 2:17) and to his undeserved suffering (Rom 15:3).
verses.21: "sour wine for my thirst:" This description applies to Jesus’ suffering (Matt 27:34, 48; Luke 23:36; John 19:28-29).
verses.25: Peter quoted this verse after the death of Judas Iscariot (Acts 1:20).
verses.28: "Erase their names from the Book of Life:" Cp. 1:5-6; 9:5; Rev 3:5; 20:15; 21:22-27.
verses.31: Making a vow often included a sacrifice (20:3; 51:19; cp. 50:13-14; 51:16).
verses.36: God’s people "will inherit the land" because the wicked will perish (see 37:8-9).
verses.1-20: These last four psalms of Book Two contrast with the psalms describing God’s mighty acts in creation and in redemption, capped by God’s march to Zion (Pss 65–68). Psalms 69–71 portray the king’s anguish, and Ps 72 responds with a prayer for God to bless the king.
verses.1-36: In this individual lament, the poet expresses his vulnerability, humiliation, and overwhelming pain, asking God to vindicate him for the sake of the righteous.
verses.1-2: The psalmist sees himself as almost drowning but still surviving chaotic forces and alienation from God (see 42:7; 69:14, 15; Isa 8:8).
verses.5-6: The psalmist confesses his "sins" and prays that God’s response to him will encourage others in similar conditions to place their hope in the Lord.
verses.7-12: Mistreated and abandoned by family, friends, and community, the psalmist turns to the Lord for comfort, relief (69:13-18), and redress (69:22-28).
verses.10-12: When the psalmist denies himself normal comforts to seek God in prayer, the wicked ridicule him.
verses.13-18: The psalmist’s only recourse is to pray for rescue and relief from his enemies.
verses.19-21: Alone and misunderstood, the psalmist confesses that he cannot bear his doubts. His heart has been broken by his problems.
verses.22-23: The psalmist wants God to transfer his suffering (69:3) to his enemies. Paul applied these words to the unbelieving Jews of his day (Rom 11:9-10).
verses.29-33: The psalmist prays that his pain will turn to praise.
verses.34-36: The psalmist prays for Zion, offering a new petition from a new circumstance. He applies the prayer (69:1-33) to the desperate condition of Judah (see 51:18-19).

verses.1: title "asking God to remember him:" The meaning of this phrase is unknown (also found in 38:title).
verses.1-5: This psalm, nearly identical to 40:13-17, contains an urgency (70:1, 5) that fits with the surrounding psalms (cp. 69:17; 71:12).

verses.9: The poet prays for continued fellowship with God (see 9:10; 51:11). In his weakness, he needs the Lord’s strength even more (see 143:7).
verses.10: In their "plotting", the psalmist’s enemies take counsel and scheme together (2:2; 21:11; 31:13; 35:4; 63:9-10).
verses.14: The psalmist contrasts his own goodness with his enemies’ evil; he centers his life in the Lord, even during hard times (see 9:17-18; 27:13-14).
verses.20: "lift me up from the depths:" The psalmist hopes for the renewal of an abundant earthly "life". This later became grounds for belief in the resurrection of the dead.
verses.21: Being assured of God’s "comfort" also assures the poet of God’s presence, care, and goodness (23:4, 6; 86:17). God’s comfort enhances the psalmist’s sense of being alive (see 119:50).
verses.1-24: This untitled lament by an aging believer is more of a confession of confidence and hope than the cry of someone abandoned by God. The psalmist experienced God’s power and protection in his youth (71:5-8) and now prays for rescue from the adversaries who stalk him in his old age (71:9-13). Even in the midst of his peril, he continues to tell of God’s past faithfulness and looks forward with hope to a time when he can testify to the next generation that God is faithful and righteous.
verses.1-4: The poet has learned to acknowledge God as the reliable rock who will do what is right toward him and his oppressors. See also 31:1-3.
verses.5-6: The psalmist has "trusted" God throughout his life (see 22:9).
verses.9-18: The aging believer turns to the Lord for hope. As questions from his adversaries get under his skin and his own strength fails, he asks God to answer his prayers. He does not seek answers to prayer for himself but so that he can tell the story to the next generation.
verses.19-21: God’s righteous character provides encouragement and strength in the midst of suffering. The wounded psalmist confesses faith in God’s ability to transform his misery and weakness into abundant life.
verses.22-24: As he awaits God’s rescue, the psalmist prepares himself to declare with instruments and voice that God is faithful and righteous.

verses.1: "love of justice . . . righteousness:" Kings in the ancient Near East were expected to represent justice; the standard for Israel’s kings was much higher because the Lord was their model.
verses.3: The administration of justice transforms the earth into fruitfulness, abundance, harmony, and goodness (see Isa 32:16-17).
verses.4: A just ruler will "defend the poor" against injustice, "rescue" them from violence, and bring "their oppressors" to account for their wrongdoing.
verses.5: "May they fear you:" In Hebrew, this clause seems to be a response to the enforcement of justice. The Greek version reads May they endure, which makes this a prayer for longevity (21:4; 72:15, 17).
verses.10: "The western kings of Tarshish" came from a major colony in the western basin of the Mediterranean. "The eastern kings of Sheba" came from an area in southern Arabia, home of the queen of Sheba (1 Kgs 10). • "Seba" was probably located somewhere south of Egypt, perhaps on the western shore of the Red Sea across from Sheba. • The "gifts" offered to the king represented a tribute and a token of submission.
verses.11: "All kings" and "all nations" must submit to the messianic king. The hope expressed in 2:10-11 will be realized (see 96:1-3; 1 Cor 15:25) when other leaders and peoples "bow before" and "serve" this king.
verses.12: To "rescue the poor" means to bring an end to the rule of their oppressors.
verses.13: Like a father, the king "feels pity" for those in need (see Mal 3:17).
verses.15: The "people" will "bless him", fulfilling God’s promise to Abraham (Gen 12:3; see Ps 133:3).
verses.16: "the trees of Lebanon:" Lebanon was renowned for its lumber (see study note on 2 Chr 2:8).
verses.20: This parenthetical note ends Book Two, which consists mostly of "prayers of David". Books Three to Five were probably compiled after Book Two; they include additional psalms of David (Pss 86, 101, 103, 108–110, 122, 124, 131, 133, 138–145).
verses.1-20: This royal psalm closes Book Two, with 72:18-20 functioning as an epilogue to all of Book Two. The psalmist reflects on the prospects of David’s royal line and on Zion (see Pss 46, 48). He prays that Israel’s kings will be good and prosperous, extending the Lord’s blessing on his people throughout the whole earth. The surpassing righteousness and dominion sought in this prayer foreshadow the coming of Jesus, the Son of David.
verses.1-7: The blessings of justice create a balance in nature, resulting in harmony, prosperity, and fertility.
verses.6-7: The administration of justice is "refreshing like spring rain", enabling the "godly" to "flourish" (see Isa 45:8) like flowers. • "until the moon is no more:" This phrase means forever (see Ps 89:36-37).
verses.8-11: The anointed king will rule over the whole world. Even hostile nations will submit to him. In the ancient Near East, bearing gifts to the king acknowledged his success and his reputation (see 1 Kgs 10).
verses.8-9: "from sea to sea:" This phrase represents the whole world. • Solomon’s kingdom extended "from the Euphrates River" in the east to the Philistine territory in the west (1 Kgs 4:21; see Pss 80:8-11; 89:19-25), where the Mediterranean Sea appeared to be at "the ends of the earth" (see 2:8). Everyone "will bow before" this king, including the "desert nomads" (72:9), "his enemies", and all the kings of the world (see Mic 7:17).
verses.12-14: The anointed king will rescue the needy. He is not only the judge but also a father to the poor (10:14, 17; 68:5).
verses.15-17: The just kingdom will be long-lasting and universal. The summary combines the themes of abundance of crops, longevity, tribute of the nations, and the prayer of the nations.
verses.18-19: This doxology concludes Book Two of the Psalter.

verses.1: People "whose hearts are pure" are renewed by God’s Spirit (51:10), commit themselves to lives of godliness, keep away from anything that is sinful, and enjoy God’s presence (see 24:3-4).
verses.6: The proud adorn themselves with "pride" and "cruelty" rather than wisdom (Prov 1:9).
verses.9: The proud "boast", claiming that they own everything and are not subject to anyone (see 2:1-3).
verses.24: The Lord leads the godly through their troubles and changes their misery into splendor.
verses.1-10: The apparent prosperity of the wicked (Ps 73) and God’s apparent rejection of his people (Ps 74) raise questions about his justice. God is sovereign over the whole world, and he determines the time for judgment (Ps 75).
verses.1-28: This wisdom psalm examines the injustice of the prosperity of the wicked. The psalmist affirms that God is good to the godly but his own experience differs (73:2-12). Nearly overcome by his doubts (73:13-16), the psalmist meets the Lord in the sanctuary and gains a perspective that stretches beyond his life and renews his confidence in God (73:17-26). His disturbing doubts stir a greater passion for truth. He knows that he can trust God and that God will rescue him (73:27-28).
verses.2-3: The poet sees the prosperity of the wicked as unfair (see 72:7) and resents it. • The psalmist’s "feet were slipping" from the way of wisdom and godliness (see 17:5; 37:31), but God kept him from falling off the trail entirely (38:16; 66:9; 94:18; 121:3). • "when I saw them prosper:" Cp. 72:3, 7.
verses.4-12: The psalmist presents a caricature of the bliss of the wicked (cp. Ps 1).
verses.13-17: Recognizing the ramifications of his discouragement and doubt, the psalmist turns to the Lord and receives special insight.
verses.13-14: These rhetorical questions expect a discouraging “yes” for an answer. The psalmist wonders if godliness has become a meaningless ritual (see Mal 3:14-15). • "My heart" refers to his whole being. • The psalmist’s "pain" comes from discipline and rebuke (Ps 39:11; Prov 1:23, 25; 12:1).
verses.15-16: If the psalmist had verbalized his suspicions about the futility of godly living, he would have discouraged God’s people and given God’s enemies an opportunity to blaspheme (cp. John 13:20). Instead, the psalmist internalizes the problem and reflects on it.
verses.17-20: At this time, God’s "sanctuary" was the Temple in Jerusalem. There, in God’s presence, the psalmist receives special insight (cp. 18:6). • God deals with the "wicked" over the long term. He waits patiently and gives them time to repent (Ezek 33:11; 2 Pet 3:9); those who do not repent will get what they deserve.
verses.21-22: The psalmist’s feelings about the prosperity of the wicked had given him a "bitter" spirit.
verses.25-26: Nothing "in heaven" or "on earth" is better than being near God.

verses.1: God "rejected" his people because their sin aroused his anger (106:34-46). • Like a tender shepherd, God cares for his people, "the sheep of" his "pasture" (Pss 23; 100:3).
verses.2: The Lord "chose" and "redeemed" Israel from Egypt in the Exodus (cp. Exod 15:13). • "your own special possession:" This is another expression for “your people” (Pss 28:9; 78:62; 94:14; 106:40).
verses.12: "my king from ages past:" The psalmist acknowledges God’s power and his historical bond with Israel (5:2; 44:4; 84:3).
verses.14: "Leviathan:" See 104:26; Job 3:8; 41:1, 12, 22, 31; Isa 27:1. Here, the creature’s multiple "heads" suggest a mythical monster.
verses.15: "springs and streams to gush forth:" God provided water in the desert for his people (see 68:8-9; Exod 17:6); he "dried up" the Red Sea (Exod 14:21) and the Jordan River (Josh 3:17).
verses.1-23: The psalmist laments the destruction of the Temple in Jerusalem (586 BC) with vivid imagery, questions, fresh memories, and a direct appeal for the Lord to act (74:19-23).
verses.1-2: In the aftermath of Jerusalem’s fall, it seemed that God had forgotten his special covenant relationship with his people.
verses.3-8: Like a guide, the psalmist points out to the Lord what took place during the destruction of Jerusalem in 586 BC.
verses.19-23: The poet urges God to act.

verses.6: No creature has the right to rebel against its Creator.
verses.1-10: This hymn of thanksgiving includes two direct messages from God that provide assurance of his justice (75:2-3, 10). The Lord rebukes arrogant people who defy him, promising to forcibly humble them (75:4-8). Together, the community and the psalmist respond with thanksgiving for God’s character (75:1, 9).
verses.2-8: The Lord will bring justice in his own time.
verses.4-5: "The wicked" arrogantly defy "the heavens"—the dwelling place of God. Through their "boasting" they insist that they are wiser than God.
verses.7-8: The Lord alone is the Judge, with the power to exalt and humble (see 1 Sam 2:7; Luke 1:52).

verses.1: title "to be accompanied by stringed instruments:" The Greek version reads for the Assyrian.
verses.3: God brings an end to the attacks of his enemies (see 46:9).
verses.4: The victorious king’s splendor, glory, and majesty are greater than anything in the created order (8:1; 29:4; 111:3).
verses.7: The word translated "feared" (Hebrew nora’) is a wordplay on the word translated “glorious” in 76:4 (Hebrew na’or).
verses.1-12: This psalm appears to celebrate a victory. The victory might have been recent, such as over the Assyrians (see note on 76:title; see also Isa 37); or the psalm might be recalling God’s great acts of rescue in the past.
verses.1-3: God’s victory over Zion’s enemies foreshadows his worldwide victory over all his enemies.
verses.4-6: The psalmist praises God for his achievement and for his "glorious" majesty.
verses.7-9: The needy await their victorious God, while the wicked stand in fear of him.

verses.3: "I think of God:" God’s people inevitably face difficult times, but recalling his mighty acts at the beginning of their relationship assures them of God’s commitment. • Feeling "overwhelmed", the psalmist is unable to deal with the crisis (142:3; 143:4).
verses.7: Feeling "rejected" (see 43:2), the psalmist asks if the situation is permanent.
verses.10: The psalmist fears that God’s "hand" of protection (44:3; 77:15; Exod 6:6) and favor (Pss 16:7-8; 110:1) is now "against" him for no apparent reason.
verses.16: "the Red Sea:" The Canaanites attributed divine power to the sea, but God is the one who made the sea and uses it for his own purposes.
verses.1-20: The psalmist laments that God has turned away from him, even though he feels innocent. He reflects on his situation (77:3, 6, 12) and finds hope (see 25:5) in remembering God’s past deeds (77:11).
verses.1-3: The "night" provides a special opportunity for prayer and meditation (77:6, 11; see 6:6; 16:7; 17:3; 30:5; 63:6; 119:55, 62, 148).
verses.4-6: As the psalmist meditates at night, he feels so disturbed that he cannot sleep or speak. He has pleasant memories of the past, but he cannot look beyond the present moment into the future.
verses.7-9: The psalmist questions his status before God.
verses.10-12: The memories of God’s mighty works in the past fill the psalmist’s mind.
verses.13-15: This central section of the poem reflects on God as the holy and powerful redeemer.

verses.2: The psalmist recites Israel’s story (78:5-72) "in a parable" in order to teach wisdom and insight. • Jesus quoted this verse to explain why he taught in parables (Matt 13:35).
verses.12: "The miracles" are the ten plagues against Egypt that God performed during Israel’s captivity (Exod 7–12).
verses.13: God "divided the sea" when Israel crossed through the Red Sea (see Exod 14–15).
verses.14: God used a "cloud" and a "pillar of fire" to guide and protect Israel in the wilderness (Exod 13:21-22).
verses.33: An entire generation died in the wilderness (Num 14:22-23, 28-35).
verses.34: "They repented:" This demonstration of zeal was not sincere.
verses.60: God "abandoned his dwelling at Shiloh" because of the people’s idol worship (1 Sam 4:11; Jer 7:12).
verses.67: "The tribe of Ephraim" was not completely "rejected", but God favored Judah (78:68).
verses.1-72: This wisdom psalm exhorts the people to learn wisdom and faithfully pass it on.
verses.1-8: The prologue is an invitation to learn wisdom.
verses.3-4: This story of what God has done should be told from generation to generation (see Deut 6:20-25; Prov 4:1-4).
verses.5-6: The telling of the story should motivate God’s people to obey what he "commanded" (Deut 6:4-9).
verses.7-8: God holds "each generation" responsible for its own response, which should be to maintain faith and "hope" (see 9:18; 27:14) and avoid being "stubborn, rebellious, and unfaithful" (see Deut 9:6-7; 10:16; 30:6; 31:27).
verses.9-11: "Ephraim", the second son of Joseph, received a special blessing from Jacob (Gen 48:15-20; 49:22-26; Deut 33:13-17). The land that his descendants received included fertile valleys and strategic roads (Judg 8:2). However, the people of Ephraim did not live in obedience to God’s gracious covenant.
verses.12-16: The focus shifts from Ephraim (78:9-11) to Israel as a whole as the psalmist reflects on God’s power in Egypt (see 81:4-7) and in the wilderness.
verses.17-31: Israel rebelled in the wilderness despite God’s abundant provision.
verses.23-25: Abundance comes through "the doors of heaven" (Gen 8:2; 2 Kgs 7:2; Mal 3:10). • Israel ate "manna" for forty years in the wilderness (Exod 16:31-36; John 6:31).
verses.26-31: God powerfully satisfied the people’s desires, but they did not respond with gratitude or faith. Therefore, God exercised his justice.
verses.32-39: Israel’s rebellion resulted in God’s judgment, but even their short-lived and insincere repentance motivated God to exercise forbearance.
verses.34-39: Israel’s continued existence, in spite of the people’s rebellion and unbelief (78:7-8), was due to God’s compassion.
verses.35-39: The Israelites "remembered" the right doctrine (9:9; 91:1), but they did not allow God to change their "hearts" (Lev 26:41).
verses.40-55: The Israelites "rebelled" even though the Lord had rescued them from powerful plagues.
verses.56-64: Israel’s rebellion desecrated the Promised Land. The people built "shrines" to false gods and worshiped "idols" (78:58) during the period of the judges (e.g., Judg 2:11; 3:7, 17-18).
verses.68-69: In the choice of "Mount Zion" instead of Shiloh as God’s "sanctuary" on earth, God moved from the north to the south (see Ps 69).
verses.70-72: The God who had turned against his "own people" (78:62) chose "David", a shepherd (Gen 46:34; 1 Sam 16:10-11), to become their "shepherd" (Ps 78:52; cp. 23:1).

verses.1: "your special possession:" This phrase might refer to the "land", the "Temple" (see 61:5), or the people (see 79:2; 78:71).
verses.6: The repentant among God’s people ask him to vent his anger not on them but on their wicked and unrepentant enemies.
verses.8: The people’s accumulation of past "sins" contributed to the Exile (2 Kgs 17:7-23; 24:3-4); however, the people perished because of their own sins (Jer 31:30; Ezek 18:20).
verses.12: The Exile resulted in national suffering and in individual searching for the Lord. • "pay back:" See 1:6; 94:2; Jer 32:18. • The expression "seven times" signifies something complete. • Israel’s "neighbors" included Edom, Moab, and Ammon (see Ps 137:7; 2 Kgs 24:2; Obad 1).
verses.1-13: This lament describes the occasion of Jerusalem’s fall in 586 BC. The early history of Israel’s rebellions described in Ps 78 provoked God’s wrath, resulting in the desolation of Zion described here as the defilement of the Temple and the disgraced bodies that littered the landscape. The psalmist then prays for forgiveness and rescue (79:8-9), as well as for God to pay back the nation’s enemies (79:12-13). Other psalms lamenting the Exile include Pss 42–44, 102, 107, 126, 137.
verses.1-4: The poet laments the desecration of the Temple and the success of the enemy.
verses.5-8: The intensity of God’s judgment surprises the people; they cry out in despair for compassion, forgiveness, and relief. Verses 6-7 are repeated almost verbatim in Jer 10:25.
verses.9-11: The people ask God to rescue them. Although Israel’s sins caused the tragedy, the "pagan nations" must also be held responsible for the bloodshed.

verses.1: title "The tune “Lilies of the Covenant”" is unknown today.
verses.3: This verse is repeated (with an increasing crescendo) in 80:7, 19.
verses.12: "broken down our walls:" God no longer defended Israel (Isa 5:5).
verses.13: The surrounding nations were ceremonially unclean, like a "wild boar" or vicious "wild animals".
verses.15: Israel was the "son" that God had brought out of Egypt (see Hos 11:1) and "planted" in the Holy Land.
verses.17: The "son of your choice" was probably the northern kingdom of Israel, although it might allude to the king of David’s dynasty (110:1).
verses.1-19: This psalm of lament might originate with the remnant of the northern kingdom after its fall in 722 BC. The people call on God as their Shepherd and as the God of Heaven’s Armies in the hope that he will return to them and restore them. They remember the Exodus and their special relationship with the Lord and conclude with an expression of renewed commitment to him (80:18).
verses.1-3: The psalmist urgently calls upon the Lord to act.
verses.1-2: God is the "Shepherd of Israel:" See also 23:1; 28:9; 78:52-53. • "radiant glory . . . power:" These expressions (145:11) refer to God’s manifest presence.
verses.4-7: The people cry out for rescue from the shame of their recent defeat. The enemy’s victory is less devastating, however, than the knowledge that they themselves are objects of God’s wrath.
verses.8-11: Israel has a glorious past, beginning with its redemption from Egypt.
verses.8-9: Israel had been a prosperous "grapevine" (Gen 1:28; Gal 5:22-23) that God "transplanted" into the land of Canaan at the time of the conquest. However, the people forgot the source of their prosperity and chose to do evil (Isa 5:1-7; Hos 10:1).
verses.10-11: Solomon’s kingdom had extended "west to the Mediterranean Sea" and "east to the Euphrates River" (see 72:8-9; 89:25; 1 Kgs 4:21).
verses.16-19: The community prays for God to change their desperate situation and restore them. They are still the Lord’s chosen people.

verses.2: An Israelite "tambourine" was a hand drum—a round frame covered with a skin, used as a percussion instrument during festivities, often to accompany dancing (68:25; 149:3; 150:4). • The "sweet lyre" and "the harp", both stringed instruments, are the instruments most frequently mentioned in the psalms (e.g., 33:2; 57:8; 71:22; 150:3).
verses.3: The "ram’s horn" mustered armies and announced special holy days (47:5; 98:6). • "new moon:" The first day of the lunar month marked "a festival".
verses.5: "for Israel:" Literally for Joseph. The tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh (the sons of Joseph) are used here to refer to the entire nation of Israel.
verses.10: God emphasizes that he and no one else "rescued" Israel. • The nation should "open" its "mouth wide" to take in God’s word (cp. Deut 8:3; Ezek 3:1).
verses.1-16: This warning message invites Israel to worship only the Lord and to enjoy the fullness of his blessing.
verses.1-3: As a prelude to the message of warning, the psalmist invites Israel to contemplate their God in song and dance.
verses.4-5: The festival, a time to celebrate and listen to the Lord, took place at God’s appointed time.
verses.6-7: The Lord heard Israel’s cry in Egypt and rescued them from oppressive slavery.
verses.8-10: God pleads with his people to remember the covenant and the Ten Commandments.
verses.11-16: The Lord helps Israel to understand that their failure was not because of his weakness.
verses.13-14: God wants to give his children his goodness, but only if they "listen" (Isa 1:18-19; 28:12; 48:18-19; see Deut 6:3). • God promises to "subdue" the "enemies" (Deut 9:3) of those who walk the "paths" of obedience and loyalty. He will also richly feed his people (Isa 1:19).

verses.1: "God presides" and stands ready to render "judgment" (see Isa 3:13). • "heaven’s court:" See Job 1:6.
verses.2: Since justice marks God’s reign (89:4), he opposes "favoring the wicked". So the psalmist is perplexed and cries out to God for justice (82:3-4, 8).
verses.5: The unjust "oppressors" cannot bring or restore order. "They wander about in darkness", unmoved by circumstances even when the whole world order falls apart around them (cp. 11:3).
verses.8: The "nations belong to" God; he will take over the realms formerly ruled by local deities and give them to his people, just as he did with the Promised Land.
verses.1-8: God condemns those who mistreat the helpless.
verses.6-7: The "gods" (see study notes on 29:1-2; 58:1), "like mere mortals", cannot escape the judgment common to human rulers. Jesus quoted from this passage in John 10:34.

verses.7: The "Gebalites" probably came from Gebal/Byblos on the coast of Lebanon. • The "Amalekites" were located south of Israel in the Negev. • "Philistia" was southwest of Judah, by the Mediterranean Sea. • "Tyre" was a port city on the Mediterranean, northwest of Israel.
verses.8: "Assyria" was northeast of Israel and north of the Persian Gulf. • The "descendants of Lot" were the Moabites and the Ammonites (83:6-7).
verses.12: The coalition’s motivation for wiping out Israel was to acquire the land (see Jer 3:19).
verses.13: "tumbleweed . . . chaff:" This dry plant material easily blows away (see Isa 17:13).
verses.1-18: This community lament asks God for rescue and victory. The terse poetry suggests difficult times. A powerful coalition desires to destroy Israel (83:1-4) and allies itself against God (83:5-8). Recalling the fate of others who came against Israel (83:9-12), the psalmist prays that the same will happen to these enemies (83:13-16) so that God will receive honor among them (83:17-18). It is unclear whether this psalm arose out of a specific historical instance of opposition by these nations, or if it is a poetic collage of nations representing Israel’s enemies.
verses.1-4: The enemy has successfully intimidated God’s people, so the poet prays that the Lord will hear and act.
verses.5-8: "signed a treaty:" The "allies" agreed to fight against God and his people. The nations that are named in the alliance were situated around Israel and Judah.
verses.6-7: The "Edomites", descendants of Esau, were located to the southeast of Judah (see Gen 25:30; 32:3; 36:1-8). • "Ishmaelites" were desert-dwelling descendants of Hagar. • "Moabites" and "Ammonites" descended from Lot; both were located to the east of Israel and Judah. • The "Hagrites" were possibly located north of the Ammonites (1 Chr 5:10).
verses.9-18: The psalmist prays that God will miraculously destroy the new coalition as he did three other enemies; doing so would bring him glory.
verses.9-11: The "Midianites", ruled by "Zebah" and "Zalmunna" and led by "Oreb and Zeeb", were Israel’s enemy in the days of Gideon (Judg 7:1–8:5). Barak’s coalition defeated "Sisera and Jabin" (Judg 4).
verses.14-15: "fire . . . fierce storm . . . tempest:" These are images of God’s manifestation in judgment (see Isa 29:6).

verses.3: The poet envies the birds that have nesting places in and around the Temple.
verses.4: The priests and Temple personnel lived in the Temple.
verses.5: Travelers needed "strength" to meet the challenges of "pilgrimage" by foot along unpaved paths, in all kinds of weather and with the possibility of assaults.
verses.6: The "Valley of Weeping" probably refers to the anguish that lonely pilgrims endured (see 23:4), rather than to an actual location. • "refreshing springs . . . autumn rains:" Even when pilgrims feel totally exhausted, the prospect of drawing near to the Lord renews their spirits (cp. Isa 35:6-10; 41:18-20; 43:17-20; 49:10).
verses.9: Both kings and priests were "anointed" to dedicate them for service (see 132:17; Exod 28:41; 1 Sam 9:16; 16:1-13; cp. Isa 61:1; Acts 10:38).
verses.10: The psalmist viewed being in God’s presence as much "better than" being "anywhere else".
verses.11: Some people worshiped the "sun" as a god, but the true God provides all that anyone needs.
verses.1-12: The psalmist expresses his deep spiritual longing for God’s presence. He faints with longing as he reflects on the Temple and on pilgrims making the journey to Jerusalem (84:1-7). He prays for himself and for the community (84:8-9). The conclusion of the psalm (84:10-12) clarifies that the Temple represents God—the psalmist truly longs for God’s presence. He knows that God’s goodness is greater than life and that only God can give his people favor and honor (84:10-11).
verses.1-4: The psalmist is far from the Temple. He turns toward it in hopeful reflection.
verses.5-7: The pilgrimage to Jerusalem reenacted the Exodus, when God marvelously provided for his people (see 78:15-16; 105:41). The psalmist imagines the pains of travel turning to the joy of arrival.

verses.1: God "restored the fortunes" of Israel by bringing the nation back from exile (see 14:7; 126:1).
verses.2: When God "forgave the guilt" of "their sins", he gave the people the possibility of fellowship with him (see 32:5).
verses.13: "Righteousness" is like a messenger preparing the world for God’s coming in response to the prayers of his people (85:4-7; 89:14).
verses.1-13: The psalmist leads the postexilic community in lament and prayer for full redemption. He ponders God’s past rescue of Israel from exile (85:1-3), longs for greater evidence of God’s goodness, and leads the community in prayer for full restoration (85:4-7). God responds with a message of peace (85:8-9), and the psalm concludes with a lyrical outburst at the grandeur of God’s salvation (85:10-13).
verses.1-5: Though the psalmist gratefully acknowledges God’s goodness, he also asks God whether his wrath will last forever.
verses.6-7: This prayer for renewal is based on God’s "unfailing love" for his people.
verses.8-9: When "God the" Lord speaks, "his faithful people" listen. He promises them "peace", meaning wholeness and well-being (see 37:11). They fear the Lord and know that he and "his salvation" are "near" to them. • The Lord does not tolerate "foolish ways", such as those that resulted in the Exile.
verses.10-13: In the glorious world of renewal and salvation, all the qualities of God’s care—"love"," truth", "righteousness", and "peace"—come together and transform the created order into something new (see Isa 32:15-20).

verses.1: title This is the only psalm connected with "David" in Book Three.
verses.5: The psalmist recounts the catalog of divine perfections (Exod 34:6-7), especially God’s willingness to forgive sin (see Pss 32:5; 85:2; 145:7-10).
verses.11: The poet responds to the Lord by seeking faithful instruction in the "truth". • An individual with "purity of heart" has integrity and wholeness (see 73:1).
verses.15: God has "mercy" on his people (51:1); he is gracious (25:6), "slow to get angry" (103:8; 145:8), and "filled with unfailing love and faithfulness" (Hebrew khesed and ’emeth; 143:1). This verse repeats a theme first expressed in Exod 34:7; Num 14:18 (cp. Pss 103:8; 145:8; Neh 9:17; Joel 2:13; Jon 4:2).
verses.1-17: The psalmist invokes God’s help and praises his character in a lament prompted by the presence of evil (86:14, 17). All people will worship the gracious and almighty God (86:8-10). To this end, the poet commits himself to a lifestyle of ethical integrity (86:11) and praising the Lord (86:12-13). The last stanza contrasts the qualities of evil people with those of the Lord (86:14-17).
verses.1-4: God’s devoted servant prays for mercy. The psalmist sees himself as a member of the covenant community and as a citizen of the world.
verses.5-7: The psalmist appeals to God to remain true to his character, which is the basis for hope.
verses.8-10: "All the nations" must submit themselves to the Lord and worship him (45:17; 117:1; 148:7-11).
verses.12-13: In anticipation of God’s rescue, the psalmist praises him and trusts in his goodness.
verses.14-17: The arrogant exist both inside and outside the community. The psalmist asks for a vision of God’s character; God is so great that just a glimpse of his goodness will shut the mouths of the wicked.

verses.1: Jerusalem was Israel’s capital and the location of the Temple, God’s earthly palace (see Ps 84).
verses.4: As great as Zion is, it will be even greater when it becomes an international city where believers from all the nations have citizenship. • God keeps a record of all who confess him as their Lord (Dan 7:10; Rev 13:8).
verses.1-7: This psalm envisions Jerusalem as the city of God where all the nations are citizens.
verses.5-6: "Jerusalem" becomes the international city where all God’s children are "citizens".

verses.1: title "Heman the Ezrahite" might be a sage from Solomon’s time (1 Kgs 4:31), a descendant of Judah (1 Chr 2:6), or a member of the Levitical family charged with singing at the Temple (1 Chr 15:17; 2 Chr 5:12).
verses.18: The psalmist restates his second and first charges.
verses.1-18: In this lament, the psalmist sees himself as cast out from God’s presence. At first, he calls on the Lord. When he finds no relief from his suffering, he presents three charges against God (88:6-7, 8-12, 13-17).
verses.1-5: The psalmist calls on the Lord for "salvation".
verses.6-7: In his first charge, the psalmist blames the Lord for his demise. God’s overpowering anger did not make sense. • The phrase "the darkest depths" implies the place of the dead (143:3; see Lam 3:6) or the depths of the sea (Pss 68:22; 69:1-2).
verses.8-12: In his second charge, the psalmist claims that God has isolated him and caused his loneliness (cp. 31:11; 38:11). Loneliness was a curse in a culture where relationships were more important than personal achievement.
verses.13-17: In his third charge, the psalmist accuses the Lord of rejecting him. The force and apparent cruelty of the psalmist’s suffering overwhelm him.

verses.1: God’s "unfailing love" gives reason to celebrate "forever".
verses.3: The Lord has "sworn" by his own holiness (89:35; see 110:4).
verses.5: Praise for God’s greatness (see 8:1) comes from the inhabitants of "heaven" who witness his "faithfulness".
verses.6: "mightiest angel:" Literally son of God (see study note on 29:1-2).
verses.12: "Mount Tabor" was in northern Israel. "Mount Hermon" formed the extreme northern border of the nation.
verses.20: "I have anointed him:" This is the verb from which anointed one (Hebrew mashiakh, “messiah”) is derived.
verses.27: David would be the most eminent of earthly kings. The Hebrew word translated "mightiest" is the same as the designation for God as “Most High” (‘elyon).
verses.29: The Lord writes his faithfulness in "heaven", on the canvas of his universe (see 89:2). He records his commitment to the dynasty of David in the same way.
