verses.35: "holiness:" The Lord is wholly distinct from the created order (22:3); his character is totally pure. He does as he pleases (115:3), and he chooses to be faithful (89:1; 115:1); therefore, he "cannot lie."
verses.38: "You are angry:" The harshness of God’s wrath perplexes the psalmist.
verses.40: "broken down the walls:" The Lord’s people are completely vulnerable.
verses.42: Although the Lord promised to strengthen David, he secretly "strengthened" David’s "enemies".
verses.50: The phrase "your servants" refers to the community loyal to the Lord.
verses.52: This doxology concludes all of Book Three (Pss 73–89); it is not intended to be read as part of Ps 89. It stands in stark contrast to the anguish and questioning of Ps 89. Cp. 41:13; 106:48.
verses.1-52: Book Three (Pss 73–89) begins and ends with weighty questions. Though Ps 89 begins with a praise-filled account of how the Lord exalted the throne of David (89:1-37), the psalmist protests the Lord’s apparent rejection of his covenant with David (89:38-51; see 2 Sam 7:8-16).
verses.3-4: The psalmist restates God’s covenant with David (see also 89:19-37).
verses.5-8: God is the absolute standard of "faithfulness", commitment, and order. The angelic beings and the heavens testify to his constancy.
verses.9-13: In this hymn, the psalmist celebrates God’s comprehensive and powerful sovereignty over nature.
verses.9-10: The Lord rules over all parts of the created order, including evil. • "You scattered your enemies:" The Lord will crush (Luke 1:51) evil powers that oppose him (Ps 2:1-3). • "with your mighty arm:" This phrase represents God’s strength (89:13).
verses.14-18: God rules wisely over creation. The qualities of "righteousness, justice," and faithfulness fit the profile of a wise ruler. The "happy" people who live under his rule enjoy his "protection."
verses.15-16: Those who are wise "worship" God, "walk" in his "light", "rejoice" in their relationship with him, and "exult in" his character.
verses.17-18: The Lord protects his people with the same power by which he established the created order.
verses.19-37: The Lord chose David as his son and as king of Israel (see 2:4-6; 2 Sam 7:8-16) to provide protection for his people.
verses.26-29: The Lord adopted David as his "son," appointed him as his commander over the nations, and promised to support him "forever." Verse 26 recalls a verse from David’s song of praise (2 Sam 22:47).
verses.30-37: The Lord disciplines but does not reject his erring children. He foresees violation of trust and subsequent punishment, but he commits himself to uphold the covenant. His fidelity to David corresponds to his faithfulness to the created order.
verses.46-47: The psalmist wonders if he will live to see the end of the Lord’s "anger". Our lifetimes are "short", like a day in the Lord’s sight (90:4, 10).

verses.1: title "Moses" led God’s people from slavery in Egypt to Mount Sinai, where he received the law and established God’s covenant with Israel. • "the man of God:" Moses enjoyed a special relationship with God (Deut 33:1).
verses.2: The Lord is the eternal God. • The Lord "gave birth to the earth" by creating it.
verses.13: The phrase "your servants" refers to the community of those loyal to the Lord.
verses.15: The psalmist calls upon the Lord to "give" the people "gladness" to replace their mourning (see 92:4-5).
verses.16: The "children" represent future generations in contrast to the generations past (90:1).
verses.17: Humans waste their "efforts" unless the Lord makes them "successful" (44:3).
verses.1-17: Although the Lord’s people have made their home in him for generations, their sin widens the gap between them and their infinite Lord. The Lord’s wrath against a person’s sin might last a lifetime and yet be only a taste of his displeasure with sin. This lamentable situation calls the community to seek the Lord’s light. Taking the first step means seeking restoration with the Lord on the basis of his compassion and love (90:13-14). He alone makes his servants glad and blesses their future generations (90:16-17).
verses.1-2: The Lord becomes the "home" of the godly; he has provided shelter for countless "generations." The word translated home is not used frequently in the Psalter. It describes a place of safety where the Lord meets his needy people and cares for them (68:5; 71:3).
verses.3-6: Unlike God, humans are mortal and transitory.
verses.7-10: Sinners cannot escape God’s wrath because the Lord sees their "sins." Their fleeting "lives" are filled with afflictions.
verses.9-10: A "groan" of sorrow (Ezek 2:10) sums up a life spent in facing the consequences of sin. • Humans cause "trouble" (see Ps 10:6) and receive "pain" in return.
verses.11-12: In the search for wisdom, no one "can comprehend" the Lord (see Isa 40:13). The appropriate human response to the Lord is godly "fear" (see Ps 60:4). The Lord alone can "teach" humans to follow the path of "wisdom" (25:4-6).
verses.13-17: The psalmist prays for the Lord’s favor and restoration.

verses.1: The "Most High" is an ancient title that expresses the Lord’s exalted status as the ruler and protector of the godly (see Gen 14:19).
verses.3: God protects the godly from "deadly disease" and even a destructive word.
verses.4: The "armor" might refer to a body shield, while "protection" refers to a small shield worn on the arm.
verses.6: The reference to "disease" represents any kind of affliction.
verses.11: "he will order his angels:" Satan cited these words when he tempted Jesus (Matt 4:6; Luke 4:10-11), but God makes this promise for those who obey him (Ps 91:14), not for those who arrogantly test him (Matt 4:4, 7).
verses.14: Those who "love" the Lord will obey him (Deut 30:20; 1 Jn 5:3) and seek his protection (Pss 91:1; 145:18).
verses.15: The Lord promises to "answer" the prayers of his people. • The Psalter often speaks of people honoring the Lord (50:15); here, God promises to "honor" the godly who risk everything for his sake (62:7; 71:21; 84:11).
verses.16: A "long life" on earth represents just a small part of the Lord’s goodness and eternal friendship (23:6).
verses.1-16: This wisdom psalm expresses confidence in the Almighty God, who provides a shelter for those who take refuge in him. They receive redemption, life, and glory from the Lord, who loves and cares for those who seek him.
verses.1-2: The Lord is an ancient "shelter" (see 90:1), open to those who seek "refuge" in him.
verses.3-4: The psalmist invites the godly to trust in the Lord and find protection in him.
verses.5-8: The godly should "not be afraid", because the Lord watches over them. These promises do not guarantee an escape from trouble, but they create an expectation of the Lord’s goodness.
verses.9-13: The poet again invites the godly to seek refuge in the Lord and enjoy the benefits of divine protection.
verses.14-16: The godly can trust the Lord’s protection and provision.

verses.1: title "on the Sabbath Day:" Jewish tradition assigned one psalm to each day of the week: Sunday (Ps 24), Monday (Ps 48), Tuesday (Ps 82), Wednesday (Ps 94), Thursday (Ps 81), Friday (Ps 93), and the Sabbath (Ps 92). This is the only psalm that indicates this use in its title.
verses.7: Even when the ungodly seem to grow luxuriantly (73:3-5), they have no future (92:9; see 1:6; 90:5-6; Isa 40:6-8).
verses.8: The transcendent Lord stays above the world of human experience. From this "exalted" place, he rules and judges (7:7), celebrates his victories (68:18; see Ps 47), comes to rescue the needy (102:19), brings an end to the wicked (92:7-8), and receives praise (148:1).
verses.10: "as strong as a wild ox:" The Lord allows the psalmist to share his exaltation (92:8), thus ensuring victory.
verses.12: Carvings of "palm trees" (1 Kgs 6:29, 32, 35; 7:36) adorned the Temple, and builders made rich use of "cedars" (1 Kgs 5:6). The trees represent the godly, who are planted in the very courts of the Temple.
verses.13: The Temple area consisted of "the" Lord"’s own house" and the "courts" that surrounded it.
verses.15: "There is no evil in him!" The Lord is consistently just; he rightly judges everyone (see Zeph 3:5).
verses.1-15: Thanksgiving and praise open this psalm. The Lord—the Most High—is faithful and just in discerning between the godly and the wicked. The godly will enjoy a glorious, vigorous future, while the wicked will perish. The wise see and understand the Lord’s works as they reveal his justice (92:6-7, 11, 15). The wicked, like grass, are quickly destroyed (92:7-10).
verses.1-3: The psalmist offers praise and thanksgiving for God’s unfailing love and faithfulness.
verses.4-7: Fools perish because they do not understand the Lord’s marvelous works and eternal plans.
verses.4-5: The Lord acts and the psalmist responds in praise (92:4). God’s actions spring from his thoughts (92:5).
verses.5-6: The Lord’s "thoughts" do not make sense to the "simpleton" or the "fool", the immoral person who desires no wisdom (Prov 1:22; 10:23).
verses.8-10: The glory of the Lord provides the reason for the poet’s renewed strength and glory, and for the imminent defeat of the enemy.
verses.11-15: The psalmist understands the Lord’s mighty acts. He shares in the glory of the wise of heart.

verses.1: "robed in majesty:" The Lord stands victorious both before and after battle (see 45:3).
verses.5: Through his stable rule and "royal laws", the Lord orders the world. • "Your reign" (literally your house): The house from which God reigns might be the Lord’s heavenly palace or the earthly Temple.
verses.1-5: The everlasting Lord gloriously establishes his kingship (cp. Pss 47, 99–100).
verses.3-4: God’s victory over natural chaos gives the psalmist confidence that the Lord will also defeat his present enemies (cp. Jer 46:8; 47:2).

verses.2: Just as the Lord’s enemies rise up against him and his people (3:7; 93:3), he must "arise" and make retribution against the enemy (see 79:12; Isa 65:6).
verses.6: "widows . . . foreigners . . . orphans:" The Lord’s law protects needy people (Deut 24:17; 27:19), but they remain vulnerable in society.
verses.7: The wicked think that they can get away with their vile acts and speech, foolishly assuming that God "isn’t looking" or "doesn’t care".
verses.9: It is preposterous that those with "ears" and "eyes" would imagine their Creator to be "deaf" and "blind".
verses.10: "punishes:" This word also carries the idea of “warns” (2:10), “disciplines” (6:1; 94:12), or “instructs” (16:7). The Lord disciplines his people to purify their character (Prov 3:11-12; Heb 12:6-11). He punishes his enemies by giving them what they deserve (Ps 1:6; Rom 6:23).
verses.11: While the Lord’s thoughts are deep, "people’s thoughts" are "worthless" (cp. 92:5; 1 Cor 3:20).
verses.13: God’s "relief" includes his comfort and rescue.
verses.14: Even when it seems that he has, "the" Lord" will not reject his people."
verses.16: Only God has the power to "stand up" to the wicked (see 2:2).
verses.1-23: This plea for the Lord’s justice includes both communal and individual expressions of lament (94:1-7, 16-23). The psalmist gives voice to the pain and suffering caused by the wicked, but he also depicts the comfort and stability of the Lord’s protection. He calls on the Lord to avenge the needy against the arrogant and foolish, he rebukes such people for their folly (94:8-11), and he pronounces a blessing on the wise (94:12-15).
verses.1-7: After the community falls victim to the "wicked" (94:5-7), they pray that the Lord will render "justice" (see 7:11; 9:12).
verses.12-15: True to his nature, the Lord rewards those who live by his wise instruction and makes them happy according to his promises.
verses.16-23: The psalmist’s prayer resumes (see 94:1-7) with a desperate cry for the Lord’s justice; it concludes with the hopeful expectation that evil will end.
verses.18-19: The psalmist’s experience of "slipping" contrasts with God’s promise to stand with him (94:12-13; see 15:5; 93:1).

verses.3: "above all gods:" The psalmist refutes idolatry and paganism (96:4-6; 135:15-18; see also Isa 46:5-7).
verses.8: To "harden your hearts" means to be stubborn and resist the Lord’s grace (see Num 20:2-13; see also Matt 13:3-23; John 12:37-43; Eph 4:17-32; Heb 3:6-19; 4:6-11).
verses.9: Israel’s "ancestors . . . saw" the wonders of the Lord, but they foolishly did not try to grasp their significance (see 92:5-6).
verses.11: The generation of Israel that wandered in the wilderness for forty years failed to enter the "place of rest" that Israel enjoyed after the conquest of the land (1 Kgs 8:56; see Deut 12:9). The Lord promised them the land and gave it to them (Isa 28:12), but they did not obey him (Isa 28:1). The warning reminds every generation of the need to obey in faith. • The rest that God provides includes peace, provision, and protection (Ps 132:14-18). The author of Hebrews challenged a new generation to enter the rest provided by Jesus Christ (Heb 3:7–4:13).
verses.1-11: This call to worship urges the people to respond to the Lord, the Shepherd, and to follow him faithfully. The previous generation, who refused to obey, did not receive the blessings of the Promised Land.
verses.3-5: The Lord is the "great King" over the whole universe.
verses.4-5: The whole created order owes its existence to the sovereign Lord alone—not to various gods.
verses.6-7: The great King cares for his people as a shepherd cares for his "flock" (Isa 40:11). • The Lord" our maker", the Creator of heaven and earth, also made a people for himself (Isa 45:9-12; 51:12-16).
verses.8-11: If people want to enter into the Lord’s rest, they need to respond immediately (see Heb 3:7–4:11).

verses.1: Three psalms open with the exhortation to "sing a new song" (Pss 96, 98, 149); the song celebrates the Lord’s universal kingship (see 33:3).
verses.4: "Great is the" Lord"! . . . most worthy of praise:" With this refrain, the poet exalts the Lord over all the gods (95:3) and nations (99:2). He inspires awe more than anyone or anything else (76:7, 12; 89:7; 99:3; 111:9). He is beyond human possession or comprehension. The story of what he does to redeem his people causes them to praise him.
verses.5: The Lord" made the heavens", an even greater task than creating the earth. The "idols", made by human hands (115:4), created nothing.
verses.6: "Honor and majesty:" The Lord is glorious (96:6; 104:1; 148:13), and so are his works in nature (8:1) and in redemption (111:3; 145:5).
verses.7: "nations of the world" (literally families of the nations): Families and clans represent subdivisions of the nations (see Gen 12:3). • The nations must respond to the Lord’s glory (Pss 8:1; 19:1-4; 24:7).
verses.8: The "courts" of God’s sanctuary were usually off-limits to non-Jewish people. In this psalm the nations of the world—the non-Jews—are invited in (65:4; 84:2, 10; 100:4; 116:19; 135:2; Isa 1:12).
verses.9: Worshipers should "tremble" in awe (96:4; see 18:7-15; 97:4) at the "splendor" of the Lord’s majesty and holiness (Heb 12:25).
verses.10: The Lord’s coming means the end of injustice. He rules fairly (9:8; 96:13; 98:9) and inaugurates an era of harmony and order not experienced since Eden. • The Lord’s reign over "the world" is founded on the strong pillars of “righteousness and justice” (89:14), so it "cannot be shaken" (cp. 11:3).
verses.12: All of nature will experience renewal in God’s presence (65:13; 72:6, 16; Isa 44:23; 55:12; Rom 8:21-22).
verses.1-13: This psalm establishes the Lord’s universal kingship (see Ps 93) and prepares for the coming of the Lord to bring justice and righteousness into the world. The psalmist invites everyone to worship the Lord (96:1-3), the glorious Creator of all the earth (96:4-6), because worship is due to him alone (96:7-9). The universe joins in praise as the righteous Judge establishes a new order (96:10-13). • This psalm (along with 105:1-15; 106:1, 47-48) is included in David’s song of praise recorded in 1 Chr 16:1-43.
verses.4-6: The gods of the nations are as nothing before the glorious and majestic Creator of the earth.
verses.11-13: The psalmist exhorts the created order to respond with joy to the news of the Lord’s coming. Cp. a similar theme in 98:7-9.

verses.1: The "farthest coastlands" represent the most remote parts of the world.
verses.6: As the Lord enters the world, the testimony of his righteousness resounds from above (50:6). • "Every nation" will view the open display of the Lord’s "glory" (see 8:1; 19:1-4a; 24:7; Isa 40:5).
verses.7: At the Lord’s coming, when "every god must bow" to him, those who worship other gods will face their own folly (see 95:3-5).
verses.11: The godly people of integrity (see Prov 2:7, 21; 3:32; 11:6, 11; 14:2), "whose hearts are right", maintain a relationship with the Lord and with others (Pss 94:15; 125:4). The wicked plan the downfall of the godly (11:2), but the Lord rescues them (11:1; 36:10). Then the sorrows of the godly turn to joy and praise (32:11; 64:10; 111:1; 119:7).
verses.1-12: God is greatly exalted over the gods and over all the earth. Awe-inspiring phenomena accompany his coming. Even the created order is visibly affected and the wicked perish, but the people of Zion love his coming and rejoice.
verses.2-4: "Dark clouds . . . Fire . . . lightning:" This language shows that the Lord is coming in judgment.
verses.5-7: The created order stirs at the coming of its King. He alone deserves worship.
verses.8-12: "Jerusalem" rejoices at the news of the Lord’s coming, for he brings justice and rescues the upright of heart.

verses.6: The Temple musicians used "trumpets" to call people together for meetings (cp. 81:3).
verses.1-9: This psalm celebrates the Lord’s kingship. The Lord is Israel’s true King, its champion and savior. His people sing a new song celebrating his victorious power and faithfulness to them. The Lord displays his righteous rule to all the nations throughout the earth, which will culminate in a worldwide kingdom of justice (98:2, 9). Consequently, all the earth must worship and rejoice together because the Lord is coming (98:4-6).
verses.2-3: The Lord makes known his righteousness and faithfulness (see also Isa 52:10).
verses.4-6: The psalmist invites the whole earth to worship the King (see 96:1).
verses.7-9: The created order is personified as rejoicing at the coming of the righteous Judge (see 93:3-4; 96:11-13).

verses.1: It is fitting to "tremble" and "quake" in response to the Lord’s holiness (see 96:9). • The "throne between the cherubim" refers to the cover of the Ark of the Covenant (Exod 25:17-22).
verses.4: The qualities of the Lord’s rule include strength, "justice", love, "fairness", and "righteousness" (see 93:4; 97:2, 6-7, 12; 98:2-3, 9; 138:6).
verses.6: "Moses" and "Samuel" were great models and leaders who had prayed on behalf of the Lord’s people (Exod 32:31-32; 1 Sam 12:23).
verses.7: The Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron from "the pillar of cloud" (Exod 33:9; Num 12:5-6), and for a time, the people responded to the revelation.
verses.1-9: The psalmist calls the nations to worship the Lord, the king of the earth who rules from Zion.
verses.1-5: The Lord is the holy and righteous King (Isa 6:1-5). Mount Zion, the location of the Lord’s Temple, metaphorically stands as the highest point on earth (Ps 113:4; Isa 2:2; 6:1). From this summit, the Great King (Ps 47:2) can see, rule over, and receive praise from all nations and peoples.
verses.6-8: God showed favor by responding to his people in the past, while holding sinners accountable.

verses.3: "The" Lord is the one who determines who "his people" are. • "the sheep of his pasture:" God will guide and protect his people (23:1, 4).
verses.4: "Gates" and "courts" were part of the Temple in Jerusalem.
verses.1-5: This psalm calls all nations to come to Jerusalem to worship the Lord and acknowledge his goodness to Israel.

verses.2: "in my own home" (literally in my house): This commitment to "integrity" might refer to private life at home. Some interpreters view my house as referring to the king’s palace; the commitment would then refer to the policies of his administration. • Leading a "life of integrity" means choosing a wise lifestyle.
verses.6: The psalmist surrounds himself with people who are also committed to integrity (101:2).
verses.1-8: This hymn expresses a commitment to live with integrity and to avoid evil. Jesus meets this ideal.
verses.4-5: The psalmist hates what the Lord hates (Prov 6:16-19; see Pss 5:5; 11:4-5). • "Perverse ideas" come from corrupt human hearts (cp. 18:26).
verses.7-8: The psalmist commits himself to ridding his "house" and "the city of the" Lord—representing the entire kingdom—of all evil.

verses.3: "Smoke" is an image of transitory life (37:20; 68:2). • The psalmist’s "bones" represent his whole being (see 6:2; 34:19-22).
verses.4: "Like" dried "grass", the psalmist senses his life ebbing away.
verses.5: "skin and bones:" The psalmist has wasted away because of his anguish (see 102:9; 109:24).
verses.6: The "owl" was associated with ruin and desolation (Isa 34:11, 15).
verses.10: The psalmist blames the Lord for his troubles.
verses.11: The psalmist’s existence seems empty and transitory (102:4; 109:23; 144:4).
verses.12: "forever . . . to every generation:" The frailty of humans (102:3-11) contrasts with the permanence of the Lord.
verses.13: "Now is the time" for the Lord to restore Jerusalem from exile (see 75:2; Jer 29:10; Dan 9:1-19).
verses.17: The people of Israel were "destitute" (or naked) during the Exile.
verses.18: "Let this be recorded:" The written record stands as a memorial to the Lord’s goodness.
verses.19: The "heavenly sanctuary" refers to God’s holy place on high (see 92:8-10).
verses.22: The "multitudes"—both Jews and Gentiles—will join in the worship of the Lord (see 96:7, 9; 106:48; Isa 2:2-4; 43:10-13; 57:15; 60:3-7).
verses.24: The psalmist draws a contrast between his days (102:23) and God’s years (cp. 90:4).
verses.28: The Lord’s "presence" provides the basis for the security and happiness of his "people" (23:6).
verses.1-28: A frail and afflicted human being prays for the Lord’s compassion on Jerusalem and for his presence with its inhabitants.
verses.1-2: The psalmist appeals to the Lord not to "turn away" (or hide your face). Israel experienced his turning his face away during their exile.
verses.7-8: The psalmist cannot sleep (see 63:6-8). Like a "bird on the roof", he feels isolated from both friends (see 88:8) and "enemies".
verses.12-17: The topic changes from the psalmist’s miseries to the Lord’s glory. A vision of the Lord’s compassionate kingship gives him confidence in Zion’s future.
verses.15-16: When the Lord arises (102:13), "the nations will tremble" with fear because they will see "his glory" (see 8:1; 19:1-4a; 24:7). The rebuilding of Zion and the Temple portray God’s glory and fulfill this promise. An even greater fulfillment will come with the New Jerusalem (Rev 21).
verses.18-22: The Lord will have mercy; Jews and Gentiles alike will worship him.
verses.23-28: Although the psalmist suffers in the present, he bases his hope for the future on the Lord’s past faithfulness.
verses.25-27: In contrast with the permanence of the Creator, the created order "will wear out like" a piece of "clothing" (see Isa 40:28). • The writer to the Hebrews describes this passage as having been addressed to Jesus, the Son (Heb 1:10-12).

verses.9: If the Lord were to "constantly accuse" or "remain angry forever", no one would be left (see Isa 54:7-8; 57:16).
verses.13: "The" Lord" is like a father to his children:" This analogy forms the basis for Jesus’ teaching about God’s fatherhood (see Matt 5:43-48; 6:1; 10:19-20; 12:50; Luke 6:36; 12:29-32; John 8:31-59; 15:1-8; see also 2 Sam 7:14; Jer 3:19; 31:9; Mal 1:6; 2 Cor 6:16-18).
verses.18: To "obey" God means to be "faithful" and loyal to him.
verses.22: God’s "kingdom" extends over all things, so all things are called to praise the Lord. • The concluding phrase takes us back to 103:1-2.
verses.1-22: This psalm celebrates the Lord’s perfection, compassion, forgiveness, and goodness.
verses.1-6: The psalmist offers praise for the Lord’s goodness.
verses.1-2: "Let all that I am praise the" Lord":" Pss 103 and 104 each open and close with this commitment (103:1-2, 22; 104:1, 35; see also 146:1).
verses.7-8: The Lord "revealed" himself "to Moses" in distinctive ways that ensured his relationship with his people (see Exod 34:6-7; Num 14:18).
verses.11-12: The Lord’s "love" and forgiveness are infinite and complete.
verses.14-16: The Lord compassionately cares for frail humans (see 37:2; 90:5; 92:7; 102:4; Isa 40:6-8).
verses.17-19: "the love of the" Lord" remains forever:" The Lord’s kingdom is everlasting, so he commits himself to his people across many generations.
verses.20-21: The psalmist exhorts the Lord’s angels, his servants and messengers, to praise the Lord.

verses.1: "Let all that I am praise the" Lord":" Pss 103 and 104 each open and close with this commitment to praise (103:1-2, 22; 104:1, 35). • "how great you are!" This acclamation expresses praise for rescue (see also 35:27; 40:16; 70:4).
verses.3: This poetic portrayal envisions "the clouds" as beams that support heaven.
verses.4: Wind and lightning are seen as divine "messengers". The Lord uses weather phenomena as he desires (77:17-18; 78:26; 135:7; 148:5-6). • The psalmist interacts with day three of creation (Gen 1:9-13). The Lord is master of water and earth.
verses.6: At first, "water" covered the earth.
verses.7: The Lord created dry ground on day three of creation (Gen 1:9-13).
verses.8: The earth originates in God’s will.
verses.9: The Lord "set a firm boundary for the seas" to protect the land. God’s sovereignty over sea and land was an argument against the existence of Baal, whom the Canaanites celebrated as victorious over the waters (see Ps 29).
verses.14: "people to use:" People are the managers of the created order, and they receive nourishment from the work of their hands.
verses.15: While both can be misused (cp. Prov 21:17), the Lord provides "wine" and "olive oil" as gifts to enhance life. Life is sustained by basic food, represented by "bread".
verses.19: "the moon to mark the seasons:" Ancient Israel based its calendar on the cycles of the moon. • "the sun knows when to set:" This is a poetic description from the perspective of normal observation. The sun goes down at a regular time every evening.
verses.25: The "ocean, . . . teeming with life of every kind" (see Gen 1:20-21), exemplifies the Lord’s creative activities.
verses.26: "ships sailing:" Commercial vessels engaged in sea trade were one of the wonders of the ancient Near East (see Isa 2:16; 23:1, 3). • "Leviathan:" The psalmist says that this feared creature is nothing but the Lord’s pet.
verses.31: The Lord reveals his presence in the created order (see 8:1; 19:1-4; 24:7) and takes "pleasure" in his new creation (see Isa 65:19).
verses.32: The trembling "earth" and the smoking "mountains" represent the Lord’s coming in judgment against sinners and salvation for his faithful people (see 18:7-15).
verses.35: The Lord will remove all forms of evil that defile his creation. • The concluding phrase takes us back to 104:1 (see also 103:1-2, 22; 146:1).
verses.1-35: This creation hymn (see also Pss 8, 33, 145) exalts God’s goodness and majesty. The psalmist reflects on the present world, the original creation, and a future new creation. He sees both creations as marvelously and wisely made (cp. 139:14), as the work of the Lord’s Spirit (104:30; Gen 1:2; 2 Cor 3:6).
verses.2-4: The psalmist interacts with two of the days of creation (see Gen 1:1-8), when God created the heavens and light.
verses.9-10: The Lord reigns over all bodies of water, including those on land. He replaced chaotic waters with order and abundance, and the earth became a splendid place for animals and humans, with water refreshing the ground, the birds, and the animals.
verses.11-18: The psalmist celebrates animal, plant, and human life, as well as the Lord’s abundant provision for all of it (Gen 1:9-30).
verses.17-18: The "storks" migrated from northern Europe and resided in Palestine during the winter. • "hyraxes:" These animals are about the size of a rabbit and live in rocky places.
verses.19-23: The psalmist rejoices in the order of night and day, marking day four of creation (Gen 1:14-19). This cycle gives all creatures an opportunity to live.
verses.20-23: Cycles of "darkness" and "dawn" mark the days on earth.
verses.24-26: The Lord’s works testify to his wisdom. All parts fit together—land and sea, night and day, land creatures and sea creatures. The Lord’s wisdom makes life orderly and wonderful.
verses.27-30: All life depends on the gracious sustenance of the Lord of life and death (cp. Matt 6:11).
verses.29-30: "When you give them your breath:" Life on earth is only possible as the Lord’s gift, symbolized by his breath (Hebrew ruakh, “breath, wind, spirit”). The Lord’s Spirit is the agent of renewal (Isa 32:15-20).
verses.31-35: The psalmist moves from describing the known creation to anticipating the new creation, when the Lord will renew the created order into a world without sinners.

verses.8: The "covenant" is the Lord’s irrevocable oath to be the Father of Abraham and his descendants (see Gen 12:1-9; 15:1-21).
verses.11: God promised "the land of Canaan" to Abraham’s descendants as their "special possession", where they could live as God’s people (105:44-45; Gen 12:7; 15:7-21).
verses.15: Abraham was one of the nation’s "prophets" (Gen 20:7).
verses.23: "Egypt" (Hebrew mitsrayim) is called "the land of Ham".
verses.37: "not one . . . stumbled:" The Lord protected all of his people (cp. 9:3).
verses.39: The Lord’s presence was as evident to all as a "fire" in the "darkness" (Exod 13:22).
verses.44: Canaan was a land of "pagan nations" (see 111:6). The psalmist might also be reflecting on God’s promise to Abraham (Gen 24:60) regarding the lands given to Isaac (Gen 26:3).
verses.45: The Lord planned for Israel to testify about him by obeying him; Israel was to be his model people.
verses.1-45: This hymn praises the Lord’s faithfulness to Abraham and his descendants in all their journeys—from Ur to Canaan (105:12), to Egypt (105:17, 23), through the wilderness (105:37, 41), and back to Canaan (105:44). All of this fulfilled the Lord’s promise to Abraham (105:9, 42), which was the basis for Israel’s very existence. Joseph, whose suffering was changed into glory, is a paradigm of encouragement for Israel (105:16-25). • Psalm 105:1-15 (along with 96; 106:1, 47-48) is included in David’s song of praise recorded in 1 Chr 16.
verses.1-5: The poet begins with the exhortation "Give thanks" (see also 106:1; 107:1; 118:1; 136:1). The other psalms continue with the refrain “for he is good!” The rest of Ps 105 tells of God’s goodness.
verses.6-11: The story of Israel is based on the Lord’s commitment to Abraham. Even when a question arises about the future of God’s covenant with David (Ps 89), God’s covenant with Abraham stands, as does the spiritual bond between God and Israel, Abraham’s descendants.
verses.16-22: These verses tell the story of Joseph (see Gen 37–41).
verses.23-25: These verses tell the story of Israel’s affliction in Egypt (see Exod 1:1-14).
verses.26-36: The psalmist recounts the story of Moses and the plagues in Egypt (Exod 7:20–12:30).
verses.37-45: The Exodus and the conquest of Canaan fulfilled God’s promise to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (105:9-10). Unlike Ps 78, the poet recites the Lord’s goodness without commenting on Israel’s history of rebellion (cp. Ps 106).
verses.42-45: The story of redemption is also the story of the Lord’s faithfulness.

verses.1: "Praise the" Lord"!" This refrain (Hebrew haleluyah) characterizes four small subgroups in the psalms: 104–106, 111–113, 115–117, 146–150.
verses.6: The story of Israel’s redemption encompasses their sinful response from the days of the "ancestors" to the present (106:43). The themes of sin and divine wrath both open and close Book Four (90:1-9; 106:6, 23, 43).
verses.9: "Red Sea:" See Exod 14:15-31.
verses.13: "They wouldn’t wait:" God’s impatient people did not trust him to work according to his will (e.g., see Exod 15:24; 16:2-3; 17:1-3; Num 14:26-45; 21:4-9).
verses.15: "he sent a plague:" See Exod 32:35; Num 11:33.
verses.22: "The land of Ham" here means Egypt (106:21).
verses.28: "the worship of Baal at Peor:" See Num 25:3; Deut 4:3.
verses.34: Israel continued to disobey the word of the Lord while living in the Promised Land. Rather than destroying the nations, Israel accepted them and their ways (see Judg 2:1-3, 11-15; 3:5-6).
verses.39: Idolatry, like "adultery", defiles God’s people (see Lev 18:24; Hos 5:3).
verses.40: God "abhorred" Israel’s sin, as he does all sin.
verses.45: "He remembered . . . and relented:" Unlike Israel, the Lord is faithful to his "covenant" (105:8).
verses.46: As harsh as the Exile was, the Lord still protected his people (see 2 Kgs 25:27-29).
verses.47: "Gather us back:" The community prays for restoration from exile (see 102:19-22; 107:3; see also Isa 11:12; 40:11; 43:5; 54:7; 56:8; 66:18).
verses.48: This doxology concludes Book Four (cp. 41:13; 89:52). • "from everlasting to everlasting!" The reference to God’s eternal nature links to the opening of Book Four (90:1-2). • "Let all the people say, “Amen!”:" The Hebrew word ’amen means “It is true.” The godly accept the Lord’s will in exile and his promise to be their God.
verses.1-48: The Israelite community in exile confessed the Lord’s goodness and justice and their own historic sinfulness. From the humble state of exile, they pleaded for redemption and restoration, asking to be gathered back from all the places the Lord had scattered them in his wrath. The psalm does not end in despair but with the memory of the Lord’s former mercy and the hope that his mercy will be renewed (106:44-48). Israel failed, but the Lord is constant. • Verses 1, 47-48 (along with Pss 96; 105:1-15) are included in David’s song of praise recorded in 1 Chr 16:1-43.
verses.2-3: Wise people who practice justice and righteousness receive encouragement to proclaim the Lord’s great acts.
verses.4-5: The poet prays individually for the Lord’s favor before leading the community confession that follows.
verses.6-13: The community joins together to confess their sins and their ancestors’ many acts of unbelief.
verses.16-18: The people became "jealous" because they presumed to have the same privileges as God’s appointed priests (see Num 16:1-35). • "the earth opened up:" See Num 16:28-33.
verses.19-23: "they bowed before an image:" The people forgot their Savior and committed the sin of idolatry (see Exod 32:1-6).
verses.24-25: The people disobeyed God’s command when they "refused to enter the pleasant land" (the Promised Land; see Jer 3:19). • "they wouldn’t believe his promise:" See Num 13:25–14:12.
verses.26-27: God’s judgment when Israel refused to obey was death and exile (Num 14:26-30). The occasion for these severe judgments seems to have been disobeying God’s word (Ps 106:24-25) and provoking the Lord’s wrath (106:28-46).
verses.28-39: Israel’s idolatry outside of the land came with them into the land. Their nature did not change; they continued to provoke the Lord to anger by their actions.
verses.30-33: "Phinehas", who executed a flagrantly apostate Israelite man (Num 25:3-8), is an even better model of "a righteous" man than "Moses", who failed "at Meribah" (Num 20:11-13).
verses.40-46: The psalmist returns to the Babylonian exile (106:26-27). The Lord judged Israel severely, but he also restrained his wrath, remembering the covenant he had made with Abraham.
verses.43-44: When Israel was "finally destroyed", the destruction was not complete. The Lord "pitied them", so he left a remnant.

verses.2: The "redeemed" might be all who came out of exile.
verses.3: "exiles:" People came from all nations where the people of Israel and Judah had been scattered.
verses.6: The psalmist does not specify the occasion of his "trouble" and "distress". The generic nature of the adversity permits readers in a variety of circumstances to identify with the laments.
verses.11: God’s "counsel" includes his instruction and will.
verses.12: Exhausted by their "hard labor" (Lam 5:13), the people "fell". While this might be expected of the wicked (Pss 9:3; 27:2), it was unlike the Israelites’ flight from Egypt (105:37).
verses.20: The Lord creates (Gen 1:3) and sustains the universe (Heb 1:3) simply by speaking (Ps 147:18); when he speaks, people are also "healed" (Matt 8:8).
verses.32: This call for public praise expands the refrains in 107:21-22 and 107:31.
verses.38: God’s presence can be seen in the abundance of his people’s "families" and "herds" (127:3; 133:3; cp. 109:8).
verses.39: People often "become impoverished" when their rulers practice "oppression".
verses.40: In his "contempt" for human rulers, the Lord rectifies their corruption on earth.
verses.41: The large "families" of "the poor" are evidence of God’s blessing.
verses.1-43: This psalm is a hymn of praise to God the Redeemer. After an introduction exhorting the redeemed to praise God for his goodness (107:1-3), the psalmist brings together four case studies of people whom the Lord redeemed from adversity (107:4-32). He then sums up the Lord’s sovereignty (107:33-42) and concludes with an invitation to discern God’s unfailing love in all areas of life (107:43).
verses.4-9: Those who were lost in the "wilderness" thank God for his rescue. The wilderness might be a metaphor for leaving the path of wisdom (1:1; Prov 4:10-15).
verses.7-8: God "led them" like a shepherd (see 23:1). • Verse 8 is a refrain that is repeated in 107:15, 21, 31.
verses.10-16: The psalmist calls for thanksgiving and praise from people in despair over the consequences of their rebellion.
verses.17-22: Fools who received what they deserved but were rescued from death offer thanksgiving to the Lord.
verses.23-32: Sailors give thanks to the Lord when he saves them from the chaos and peril of the sea.
verses.25-29: The same God who speaks and brings about the sailors’ distress can also calm the storm with just a word (cp. Jon 1:4; Matt 8:26).
verses.33-42: These two sections (107:33-38, 39-42) expand the theme of the Lord’s sovereignty over things that humans cannot control.
verses.33-35: The Lord can choose to make the earth fertile or barren (74:15; Isa 35:6-7).
verses.42-43: Justice prevails in God’s world (1:6), and Israel’s history demonstrates God’s faithful love.

verses.1-13: This psalm combines two excerpts from David’s other psalms (cp. 57:5, 7-11; 60:5-12).

verses.1: The psalmist sees no evidence that God cares (see 28:1).
verses.8: The wicked person apparently held a "position" of leadership. Peter referred to this psalm in regard to Judas Iscariot (Acts 1:20-26).
verses.13: If one’s "family name" was "blotted out", it meant there was no "offspring" to carry on the family name or remember its history (see Prov 10:7).
verses.14: Children inherit the sinful nature of their parents (51:5; Exod 20:5; Eph 2:3). The speaker wants the Lord to punish the perpetrator for the guilt of family members who went before him (cp. Matt 23:35-36).
verses.16: The defendant committed capital crimes and did not exercise even basic decency.
verses.18: "Cursing" is the accused person’s whole way of life.
verses.20: The psalmist appeals to the principle of retribution (see 94:23).
verses.21: The Lord’s "reputation" is at stake. If the wicked triumph, others could think that the Lord is also wicked and be drawn to that wickedness (1:1).
verses.23: A "shadow at dusk" suggests a transitory, empty existence (102:11; 144:4); a single "locust" could easily be "brushed off" one’s clothing.
verses.28: The Lord’s "servant" demonstrates loyalty and obedience.
verses.29: The psalmist had been accused of being clothed with curses (109:18); now he asks that his accusers be "clothed with disgrace" and "humiliation".
verses.1-31: The psalmist begins this lament with a general charge against his accusers: They do evil in return for good (109:1-5). At the end of the psalm, he turns to the Lord in prayer, asking for his protection (109:21-25) and vengeance (109:26-31).
verses.4-5: The psalmist’s acts of kindness and godliness (see 35:12-14) have only met with stubborn opposition and expressions of hatred.
verses.6-19: The NLT translates these verses as the words of the psalmist’s accusers; Hebrew lacks "They say", which makes it unclear who is speaking.
verses.8-11: Family members of those guilty of capital crimes often died with the perpetrator (Num 16:1-33; Josh 7:1-25) or had their property confiscated (1 Kgs 21:13-16).
verses.21-25: Vulnerable and miserable, the psalmist appeals to his Lord for help. The accusations have killed his inner spirit and even his physical stamina.
verses.26-31: These verses form a prayer for God’s presence and for vindication. The psalmist wants everyone to see that he is vindicated by the Lord, not by any human agent.

verses.1: The king of Israel had the great privilege of being the Lord’s adopted son (Ps 2; 1 Chr 22:10), but he fell (Ps 89). This decree restores and heightens his position. • "The" Lord":" Hebrew Yahweh, the name of God (see Exod 3:6-14; 6:2-8; 20:2). • "my Lord" (Hebrew ’adoni) means “my master” or “my superior.” The psalmist viewed God’s messianic ruler as his superior. The New Testament frequently cites this psalm to validate Jesus’ claim to be the Messiah (Matt 22:44-45; Mark 12:36-37; Luke 20:42-44; Acts 2:34-35; Heb 1:13). • The Lord’s "right hand" represents his authority, strength, presence, and benefits. The Lord chose the descendant of David and raised him up to be close to him (Ps 80:17). Jesus claimed this position for himself (Matt 26:64; Mark 14:62; 16:19; Luke 22:69), and the apostles announced that Jesus, having ascended to heaven, sits at the right hand of the Father (Acts 2:33; 5:31; 7:55-56; Rom 8:34; Eph 1:20; Col 3:1; Heb 1:3; 8:1; 10:12; 12:2). • Ancient Near Eastern kings were sometimes portrayed as placing their feet on the backs of their conquered "enemies" as on a "footstool" (see Heb 10:12-13).
verses.4: The Lord had made an unbreakable "oath" and covenant, so his apparent rejection of David’s dynasty (89:38) in the Exile had led to a crisis. The placement of Ps 110 in Book Five reaffirms the future of the dynasty: David’s descendant must conform to God’s standard of integrity (Ps 101). His ministry will be transformed as he serves under God’s kingship (Pss 93–100). • "You are a priest forever:" The role of God’s messianic ruler changes. The priestly kingship of David and his descendants extended to serving as patrons of the Temple. David had the Ark brought to Jerusalem (2 Sam 6:15) and arranged for the Temple service (1 Chr 6:31-48; 15:11-26; 16:4-42; 23:4-32; 25:1). Solomon supervised the Temple construction (1 Kgs 5:1–7:51). Even so, Israel’s kingship was separate from its priesthood. In the messianic kingdom, the king would also minister as priest, as "Melchizedek", king of Salem (Gen 14:18), had done. The New Testament develops the ministry of Jesus Christ as a fulfillment of this new order (see Heb 5:6-10; 6:20–7:25).
verses.7: God’s messianic ruler obtains victory as a vigorous person, as if he had received nourishment "from brooks along the way" (110:3).
verses.1-7: Jesus and the apostles cite this psalm to explain Jesus’ unique ministry and status as the Messiah (Matt 22:43-45; Acts 2:32-36). It reaffirms God’s covenant with David and gives hope for the future (see 2 Sam 7:8-16).
verses.2-3: The "kingdom" will expand and increase, beginning from Jerusalem, until all enemies are conquered.
verses.5-7: The new priestly role of David’s descendant does not rescind his old role as conquering ruler. He must still bring the nations under his rule (110:2-3; see Ps 2).
verses.5-6: "at your right hand:" This position brings help and protection (see 16:7-8; 108:13). • The Lord "will strike down" rebellious "kings". Rebellion against the Lord is a capital offense (Ps 2; Rom 6:23).

verses.5: God takes care of his people’s needs, even providing "food". He "remembers his covenant" with Abraham (see 105:8-11).
verses.9: The people of the Exodus generation went free because of God’s grace.
verses.10: "True wisdom" is the source of life (Prov 3:18; 9:11; Eccl 7:12); it begins with the "fear of the" Lord (Prov 9:10).
verses.1-2: The refrain "Praise the" Lord"!" (Hebrew haleluyah) characterizes this group of psalms.
verses.1-10: This wisdom psalm contains many references to the works of the Lord that reveal his character. God is righteous, gracious, compassionate, faithful, just, trustworthy, upright, holy, and awe-inspiring (111:3, 4, 7, 8, 9). God’s character gives hope in the covenant relationship (111:5). He rescued Israel from Egypt (111:9), gave them the land (111:6), and provides for his people (111:5). However, God demands that the beneficiaries of this relationship also be people of righteousness and integrity.
verses.1-5: The godly praise God and delight themselves in his great works. His mighty acts reflect his righteousness, grace, and compassion (see 116:5-7). All who submit themselves to him experience his glory.
verses.6-8: Giving Israel "the lands of other nations" was "just and good" because the Lord was executing his justice on those he dispossessed and showing grace to the Israelites. However, if the Israelites do not live "faithfully and with integrity", they will also be dispossessed. The Lord’s people must reflect his character.

verses.6: The honesty and compassion of the wise keeps them from stumbling (15:5; 37:23-24), ensuring that they "will be long remembered" (Prov 10:7).
verses.8: Because the godly joyfully expect God to prevail and rescue them, they "face their foes triumphantly" (59:10; 112:4; 118:7).
verses.9: Paul quotes this verse in his instructions about generous giving (2 Cor 9:9).
verses.10: The "wicked . . . grind their teeth in anger" out of their bitter envy (35:16; 37:12). The vigor and reputation of the godly cause conflict with those who want them dead. • The wicked "will slink away" out of fear and shame.
verses.1-10: This psalm reiterates the themes of wisdom and the fear of the Lord (Ps 111). The wise have reason to be happy (112:1-5) and vigorous (112:6-10).
verses.1-5: The fear of the Lord leads to a life of wisdom that honors God and blesses the family and community. The godly joyfully imitate God; their obedience is not slavish.
verses.2-3: "successful:" All will know the "children" of "godly people" (see 127:4) because the godly leave a legacy for their children (see 1:3; cp. Matt 6:20).
verses.4-5: The godly imitate God by being "generous, compassionate, and righteous" (51:1; 111:1-10; 2 Cor 9:9). They "lend money" to the poor without charging interest (Pss 15:5; 112:9; Exod 22:25).

verses.4: The Lord’s glory reaches to the "heavens" (57:5, 11; 99:2; 108:5; 138:6; Isa 6:1; 57:15) and throughout the world of human relationships.
verses.6: The Lord "stoops" to the world’s level to be directly involved with his people (see 138:6; Phil 2:6-8).
verses.9: A "childless woman" was customarily treated with disdain (Gen 16:4); the Lord has the power to make her "a happy mother", as he made Sarah (Gen 21:2), Rebekah (Gen 25:21), Rachel (Gen 30:23), and Hannah (1 Sam 1:20). • God’s greatness and goodness provide ample reason to "praise" him.
verses.1-29: These psalms form what is known as the “Egyptian Hallel” (hallel means “praise”) because Jews use the collection in the celebration of Passover, which was instituted at the beginning of the exodus from Egypt. Psalms 113–114 are recited before the Passover meal and Pss 115–118 afterward.
verses.1-9: This hymn of praise exalts the greatness of the Lord’s name and glory. God is greatly exalted and glorious in heaven (113:4); he also stoops down to take care of the lowly and needy on earth (113:5-9).
verses.1-3: "The name of the" Lord (Hebrew Yahweh; see Exod 3:15) reveals his being, character, and reputation. He is exalted in time ("now and forever") and in space ("from east to west").
verses.5-9: The incomparable Lord intimately involves himself in caring for people on earth.
verses.7-8: These phrases are a quotation from Hannah’s prayer of praise (1 Sam 2:8-9a).

verses.8: The Lord miraculously provided for his people in hard times after the Exile, just as he had done in the wilderness after the Exodus.
verses.1-8: This lyrical celebration of the Lord’s power in nature recalls Israel’s beginning as a nation at the Exodus (114:1-2) and upon their entry to the Promised Land (114:3-6). It promotes reverence for the God of Jacob (114:7-8).
verses.1-2: At the time of Israel’s exodus from Egypt and their entrance into the Promised Land, Israel was one holy "kingdom" (Exod 19:5-6). • The separate references to "the land of Judah" and "Israel" indicate that the psalm was composed after the kingdom was divided (1 Kgs 12:16-17; cp. 1 Sam 11:8; 1 Kgs 1:35), and probably after the Exile. The "land of Judah became God’s sanctuary" because the people worshiped God; his Tabernacle and later his Temple were located there.
verses.3-4: "hurried out of their way!" The waters divided for Israel to escape Egypt (77:17-18; Exod 14). • "The Jordan River turned away" when Israel arrived to cross over (see Josh 3). • "skipped like rams:" God’s presence caused the mountains to quake (Exod 19:16-20).

verses.8: Worshiping idols leads one astray and corrupts those "who trust in them" (Isa 44:20).
verses.1-18: In this hymn of thanksgiving for God’s blessings, the community ascribes all glory to the name of the Lord, who is the true source of hope and blessing. Meanwhile, those who trust in idols are greatly disappointed. The blessing of the Creator of heaven and earth extends to future generations (115:14), and especially to the priesthood (115:12).
verses.1-3: The community confesses their faith that God will rescue them for the glory of his name.
verses.2-3: "Where is their God?" People deny God’s presence or power when he does not act as they think he should (cp. 14:1; 42:3, 10). However, "God is in the heavens"—he has all power, authority, and knowledge. He "does as he wishes", not what people think he should do. He works out his plans in accord with his will (Eph 1:11) and acts in his own time and in ways he chooses.
verses.4-11: This entire section is repeated in 135:15-20. • Unlike the Lord (95:3-5), "idols" cannot do anything; they are good for nothing.
verses.9-11: "Israel . . . priests . . . you who fear the" Lord":" The psalmist calls on all those in the God-fearing community to commit their ways to the living God. The threefold address assures them that the Lord is their true "helper" and "shield" (cp. 118:2-4).
verses.12-13: The groups named in 115:9-11 receive assurance of the Lord’s blessing, regardless of their social status (see 113:8).
verses.14-15: The psalmist blesses (107:37-38, 41) all who trust in and fear the Lord. The Creator will care for the families of those who fear him. • "who made heaven and earth:" This statement speaks of the Lord’s all-encompassing power in creation.
verses.16-18: "The heavens belong to the" Lord":’s:" God’s exaltation begins in heaven (113:4), far above the gods of the nations. Of course, the earth also belongs to him (47:9; 95:4). • The "dead" cannot participate in God’s blessings. The living "praise" God in thanksgiving for his blessings (79:13).

verses.1: "I love the" Lord":" This unique opening expresses affection for and commitment to the Lord (see 18:1; Deut 6:5) on the basis of what the Lord has done.
verses.2: Because the Lord responds to the cry of his people (107:41; 113:6-8), the psalmist now strongly believes in prayer.
verses.3: It isn’t clear if the psalmist’s crisis was a literal near-death experience or if he was using the term figuratively.
verses.4: This is the first of three times that the psalmist calls on the Lord’s "name" (i.e., reputation).
verses.6: People with "childlike faith" readily receive his wisdom and instruction (19:7-11; Matt 18:3-4).
verses.9: "I walk in the" Lord"’s presence:" The psalmist already lived with integrity, but since his experience of deep distress, he now enjoys open fellowship with the Lord (see 56:13; cp. Job 42:5).
verses.10: "I believed in you:" Paul quotes this phrase in 2 Cor 4:13.
verses.1-19: This hymn of thanksgiving rejoices in God’s character and in rescue from death (116:1-11). It gives an assurance of God’s protection in life and reminds the godly that the Lord watches over them even at death. The psalmist commits to living as God’s servant and resolves to honor him publicly (116:12-19).
verses.1-4: The psalmist praises the Lord for answering his prayers and rescuing him from death.
verses.5-7: The gracious, righteous, and compassionate Lord (see 111:1-5) rescued and gave rest to the psalmist.
verses.8-11: The psalmist’s near-death crisis made him more aware of life and of walking before the Lord. Though he had been in anguish, the Lord was faithful. However, "people are all liars".
verses.12-14: The Lord’s gracious gifts are so great that the psalmist can do nothing to repay his debt. Keeping his promises publicly demonstrates his gratitude. • "All he has done for" the psalmist includes answers to prayer, rescue, and life. • The "cup of salvation" overflows with God’s blessings (23:5), unlike the cup of judgment (75:8). • The psalmist makes "promises" (“vows,” 116:18) to praise the Lord publicly (116:17-18).
verses.15-19: No one lives or dies outside of God’s will. Having been given a second chance at life, the poet readily commits himself to the Lord with renewed acts of public devotion.

verses.1: Paul quotes this verse to show that Gentiles would eventually praise the God of Israel (Rom 15:11).
verses.1-2: This psalm, the shortest in the Psalter, invites "all . . . people of the earth" to "praise the" Lord because of his "unfailing love" and enduring "faithfulness".

verses.22: The "cornerstone" (or keystone) of a building or an arch gives the structure its shape and foundation. It is the most important of all the stones. The Lord chooses and places this stone for his sanctuary (Isa 28:16). Jesus referred to himself as this cornerstone (Matt 21:42; Mark 12:10-11; Luke 20:17; see Acts 4:11; Eph 2:20; 1 Pet 2:6-7).
verses.24: "This is the day the" Lord" has made:" The day of the Lord’s victory has already arrived, although its completion awaits another day (118:25).
verses.26: The "one who comes in the name of the" Lord brings the Lord’s complete victory (see 118:10-12). • During Jesus’ triumphant entry into Jerusalem, the crowds called out various blessings, including phrases taken from this verse (Matt 21:9; Mark 11:9; Luke 19:38; John 12:13). Jesus himself quoted this passage as he wept over Jerusalem (Matt 23:39; Luke 13:35).
verses.1-29: With an exultant testimony, the psalmist gives thanks for the Lord’s goodness and encourages others to trust in his faithful love (118:1-4, 29). This poem is the last of the Egyptian Hallel (Pss 113–118).
verses.2-4: "Israel . . . Aaron’s descendants . . . all who fear the" Lord":" These three groups represent the whole of the covenant community (cp. 115:9-11; 135:19-20).
verses.5-9: The Lord alone is the psalmist’s helper.
verses.6-7: "The" Lord" is for me:" Cp. Rom 8:31; Heb 13:6. • God’s presence cancels out the need to fear "mere people" (Ps 56:11). The psalmist joyfully expects God’s rescue (59:10; 112:8).
verses.8-9: Trusting in the Lord is better than placing confidence in even the most powerful human leaders (118:6; 146:3).
verses.10-12: Strength comes in the name of the Lord, declared by the threefold mention of the attackers, the Lord’s name, and victory. • Even when hostile people "blazed . . . like a crackling fire", the Lord caused them to subside like burning thorns (see Isa 9:18; 10:17).
verses.14-18: The psalmist celebrates the victory of the Lord’s "strong right arm", which kept him from death.
verses.17-21: God has restored the psalmist from death to life, so he praises the Lord publicly (cp. 116:6, 12-19).
verses.22-24: The psalmist sees his own salvation as the beginning of a new day in which the Lord will do great things.
verses.25-29: The psalmist concludes with prayer and thanksgiving, anticipating an even greater revelation of God’s victory and rescue.

verses.4: To "keep" God’s "commandments" means to guard them by obeying them.
verses.9: A "young person" tends toward foolishness (Prov 22:15) and can easily make mistakes that destroy his life (Prov 7:6-23). Youth is also the best time to develop personal discipline and pursue wisdom (see Ps 34:11; Prov 1:4). • To "stay pure" means to remain uncorrupted by wickedness and sin and to develop the integrity of life defined in Ps 15.
verses.10: The student asks God the teacher to discipline him so that he will not "wander".
verses.14: God’s wisdom is far greater than any "riches" humans seek (119:72, 127; Prov 3:14-15).
verses.15: The way of wisdom includes meditating on God’s "ways" (see 119:1, 3). The wise reflect on the implications of God’s word.
verses.29: "lying to myself:" Self-deception is a fruit of sinful human nature (Jer 17:9); it leads to folly. • Access to God’s word is a "privilege", not a right.
verses.36: The "love for money" can lead to sin (cp. Exod 18:21; 1 Tim 3:1-5; 6:10).
verses.52: The "age-old regulations" are the Torah (God’s “instructions” or “law”), a term that refers to the books of Genesis—Deuteronomy.
verses.61: "Evil people try to drag" him" into sin", but the psalmist’s memory of God’s word keeps him standing firm (see 119:16).
verses.64: God’s goodness "fills the earth"; the whole created order provides evidence of his goodness (see Isa 6:3; 11:9).
verses.95: The "wicked" intended to "kill" the psalmist, but destruction (1:6) was their own fate.
verses.96: "Even perfection has its limits:" Humans cannot fully understand God’s ways (see Eccl 3:11).
verses.113: The godly hate the wicked and their deeds (5:4-6; cp. Ezek 33:11).
verses.125: Simply possessing God’s law does not provide any benefits. The psalmist knows that only as the Lord gives "discernment" will he "understand" it.
verses.139: The psalmist’s "indignation" (cp. 69:9) comes from seeing the wicked disregard God’s word.
verses.141: The psalmist is greatly troubled by his oppressors (see 119:143; cp. Isa 53).
verses.176: God, the Great Shepherd, seeks out his "lost sheep" (23:1; Luke 15:4-6).
verses.1-176: This psalm combines elements of wisdom, lament, praise, thanksgiving, and confession. Eight Hebrew words are used frequently, translated as “instructions,” “laws,” “words,” “regulations,” “statutes,” “commands,” “decrees,” “commandments,” and “promises.” Together, these words encourage love for and obedience to God’s instructions, as found in the Scriptures (see 2 Tim 3:14-17). The expression of deep commitment to these instructions unifies the psalm.
verses.1-8: Aleph (א): God, the author of these "instructions", commands that his followers live by them. The psalmist prays to be given the grace to live by that revelation.
verses.1-4: The wise are happy. They are "people of integrity" (see 84:11) who "follow" the path of divine instruction. They "obey" God’s revelation and "search" for it "with all their hearts" (see 27:7; 119:10, 45, 94, 155), and they reject all forms of evil. Cp. 1:1-2.
verses.9-16: Beth (ב): The psalmist is determined to pursue purity and encourages the cultivation of wisdom through God’s principles (119:9) and instructions (119:10-16).
verses.17-24: Gimel (ג): Like a "foreigner" in hostile territory, God’s "servant" needs God’s guidance.
verses.17-18: The psalmist seeks to please the Lord with a full and obedient life of praise (118:17; 119:25, 77, 116, 144, 175). Only the Lord can remove his adversaries and enable him to "see" the wonderful truths found in God’s instructions.
verses.20-21: The "arrogant" are probably those who mock the psalmist (119:22-23).
verses.23-24: Those who "meditate" on God’s instructions receive "wise advice" from them.
verses.25-32: Daleth (ד): Though the poet feels anguish and sorrow, he entreats the Lord to revive him because he wants to obey the Lord. Suffering and death may result from the Lord’s chastening (118:17-18; 119:67, 71, 75), but his instruction revives the weary soul (see 119:12).
verses.33-40: He (ה): As a student, the poet asks his teacher, God, to renew life and to transform disgrace into righteousness.
verses.41-48: Waw (ו): The psalmist prays that God’s word would continue to be the source of his "love" and "salvation".
verses.41-43: The psalmist asks to be saved from enemies who speak harshly (see 42:10; 44:16; 89:50-51; 102:8).
verses.44-46: The psalmist is determined to obey the Lord.
verses.47-48: The psalmist finds "delight" in God’s word in spite of pain (119:92, 143).
verses.49-56: Zayin (ז): The psalmist asks God to "remember" his word as the psalmist also remembers God’s word and his name. Remembrance expresses devotion.
verses.57-64: Heth (ח): The psalmist seeks God’s favor and "unfailing love". Although surrounded by evildoers, he remains a loyal servant of the Lord.
verses.65-72: Teth (ט): The psalmist describes himself as a penitent sinner who gratefully accepts the Lord’s discipline.
verses.65-68: "Good judgment and knowledge" come from wisdom (111:10). • The psalmist admits that he "used to wander off" like a stray sheep (119:176). • "you disciplined me:" See 119:25-29. • "You are good and do only good:" God’s character is perfect (97:2; Jas 1:17; 1 Jn 1:5).
verses.73-80: Yodh (י): In this prayer for comfort and compassion, the psalmist commits himself to his Creator, who has afflicted him. He wants God to pay back his enemies for the wrongs they have done. He also prays to receive the gift of life. He not only prays for himself but also considers the whole community of the godly, asking that God’s answers to prayer would encourage them.
verses.73-76: As God’s child, the psalmist asks for divine wisdom.
verses.81-88: Kaph (כ): The psalmist is "worn out" from "waiting" for the Lord, but his "hope" is in God’s future "rescue".
verses.85-88: God’s word is "trustworthy", in contrast to the deceptions of the enemies "who hunt" the psalmist "down without cause" (see 119:78).
verses.89-96: Lamedh (ל): The stability of God’s wisdom gives understanding. God’s word provides order and a framework for living, even when under pressure from adversaries.
verses.97-104: Mem (מ): The instruction and wisdom of God through his word are far superior to the best that human teachers can offer.
verses.97-102: "make me wiser:" God’s word provides wisdom and perspective. God is the true source of wisdom.
verses.103-104: Wisdom is preferable to even the finest food (19:10; 81:16). • The psalmist had already rejected the delusion offered by the way of folly (see 119:18, 78, 86, 163).
verses.105-112: Nun (נ): The psalmist’s devotion to God’s word comes from within his being (119:112) and guides his external life.
verses.105-106: The Lord’s "word is a lamp" that provides perspective, hope, and guidance in darkness (18:25-29; 119:130). Even more, this "light" gives life (Prov 6:23).
verses.108-112: "offering of praise:" This Hebrew expression is unique in the Old Testament (cp. 50:23). • The psalmist is vulnerable to his opponents because of his commitment to a wise life.
verses.113-120: Samekh (ס): The psalmist declares his hatred of evil and his love for God and his ways.
verses.121-128: Ayin (ע): The servant of the Lord strains to endure the evil around him. He boldly petitions the Lord to rescue him immediately!
verses.129-136: Pe (פ): The psalmist prays earnestly for God to speak to him as he suffers from his adversities.
verses.137-144: Tsadhe (צ): God is righteous, and his word is right and just, especially in contrast to the deceptions of the wicked.
verses.145-152: Qoph (ק): The psalmist prays to the Lord at night. Although God appears to be distant, he is nearby.
verses.145-148: "I pray" and "I cry out" translate the same Hebrew verb. • "I rise early" and "I stay awake" translate the same Hebrew verb.
verses.150-151: "Coming to attack me" (or are coming near to me) is a Hebrew wordplay on "but you are near". The wicked remain far from God’s instructions, whereas the psalmist stays near, so he does not need to fear.
verses.153-160: Resh (ר): This petition for "life" can be found throughout Ps 119, but it is concentrated in this stanza.
verses.161-168: Shin (ש): The psalmist looks beyond his adversaries to the peace of God. This perspective allows him to praise God throughout the day.
verses.161-164: "my heart trembles . . . I rejoice:" Fear, trembling, and joy mark the psalmist’s devotion to God. • God’s word is a "treasure". • In the Old Testament, "seven" signifies wholeness.
verses.169-176: Taw (ת): God’s servant petitions the Lord one final time; he still feels like a lost sheep.

verses.5: "Meshech" was a Japhethite territory far to the north of Canaan. "Kedar" was an Ishmaelite territory in Arabia. Violent people lived in both locations. Meshech was the home of a famous slave trade (Ezek 27:13; cp. Exod 21:16) and Kedar of renowned warriors (Isa 21:16-17). These places can be understood as representative of the apostate, violent land where the psalmist suffered.
verses.1-3: These short, appealing songs were sung during pilgrims’ journeys to Jerusalem for the national festivals three times per year (Deut 16:16). The title of these psalms includes the Hebrew word for stairs, which some take to mean “ascending to Jerusalem.” These psalms (sometimes called the Songs of Ascents) take the reader on a pilgrimage to Jerusalem to praise God for his goodness to Israel throughout history.
verses.1-7: This short, individual lament expresses the psalmist’s trust that the Lord will deal with deceptive evildoers. It also laments living as a stranger among hateful liars. The psalmist’s picture of his life in a foreign land might have been a reality as he set out for Jerusalem, or it might depict his feelings and concerns as he begins his pilgrimage. Overwhelmed with injustice, he trusts God and looks forward to arriving in the Lord’s presence.
verses.1-2: The psalmist is surrounded by "liars", so he makes his lament "to the" Lord, the only one who can help him.
verses.3-4: The psalmist dialogues with the liars who surround him. He feels reassured that the Lord will judge them. • The Divine Warrior (see 7:12-13; 11:4-6) will throw "sharp arrows" and "glowing coals" on the liars.
verses.5-7: The psalmist feels the anguish of alienation, isolation, and perpetual conflict.

verses.1: "The mountains" were known for their idolatrous worship (Deut 12:2), and Israel was enticed to the hilltop shrines (Hos 4:13). This verse can be understood as a rhetorical question expecting a negative answer: The gods of the hilltop shrines cannot rescue anyone. Others understand the mountains to be a symbol of the Lord’s strength (Ps 95:4). In that case, the question would be interpreted literally (Where does my help come from?), with the answer given in the next verse
verses.4: God "watches over" his own, even and especially when they face many troubles (12:5, 7; 69:29; 91:14; 146:9).
verses.1-8: The leader of the group of pilgrims uses word pictures to assure the group of the Lord’s presence during the journey.
verses.4-6: The Creator (121:2) is the guardian of Israel. • God "stands beside" Israel, supporting and caring for the godly (see 16:7-8). • Both the "sun" and the "moon" were regarded as deities in the ancient Near East, but the Creator limits their power. They, too, praise the Lord (148:3).

verses.1: The central sanctuary was the "house of the" Lord. This phrase originally referred to the Tabernacle (Exod 23:19; 34:26).
verses.2: Several psalms celebrate or look forward to being "inside" the "gates" of the city (9:14; 87:2; 100:4; 118:19).
verses.3: In the time of David and Solomon, "Jerusalem" was renowned as a place of security (1 Kgs 10:6-7).
verses.4: Each of the people of "Israel" belonged to one of the tribes, and all of the "tribes" belonged to the Lord. • To "give thanks" is to present an offering acceptable to the Lord (50:14, 23; 100:4; 118:19). • "as the law requires of Israel:" See Exod 23:17; Deut 16:16.
verses.5: "the thrones where judgment is given:" In the eras of "David" and Solomon (1 Kgs 3:28), Jerusalem was the home of wisdom and justice; it would be so again (Isa 9:7).
verses.1-9: Jerusalem is here idealized as the city of God, the city of David, and the city of faith. A group of people on a pilgrimage joyfully arrive in the city (122:1-2). The psalmist sings an ode to Jerusalem (122:3-5) and prays for the city’s peace (122:6-9).
verses.3-5: Jerusalem is a metaphor for God’s heavenly dwelling. David was the archetype for God’s chosen rulers.
verses.6-9: Prayers for the "peace" of Jerusalem are motivated by love of family and God’s sanctuary.

verses.1-4: This lament on the psalmist’s lowly position expresses vivid trust in the Lord (123:1-2). The psalmist prays for God’s favor on the community, as the reality of evil surrounds them (123:3-4). The poet looks beyond Jerusalem (Ps 122) to God’s throne "in heaven."

verses.1-8: This thanksgiving song describes what might happen if the Lord were not present with his people.
verses.1-2: The negative rhetorical questions emphasize the positive idea that the Lord was indeed on their side.
verses.4-5: "the raging waters of their fury:" The enemies could have "overwhelmed" the Israelites and wiped them out if the Lord had not been with his people (cp. 69:15; Jer 46:8).
verses.6-8: The enemies of God’s people, like lions or bears who "tear" their prey with their "teeth" (see 57:4; Prov 28:15), had their mouths shut by the Lord (Dan 6:22).

verses.2: "surrounds:" God guards and protects like a wall of fire (Zech 2:5).
verses.3: The "godly might be tempted" through peer pressure and cultural domination.
verses.1-5: The psalmist expresses the community’s confidence in the Lord’s protection (125:1-2) and prays for peace (125:3-5).
verses.4-5: People who reject the straight path of the upright are fools (Prov 2:12-15). God pours out his goodness on the godly (see Ps 122:6-9).

verses.1-6: This hymn celebrates Israel’s return from exile (126:1-3). The psalmist prays for full restoration (126:4-6).
verses.1-3: The Lord brought about Israel’s restoration from exile, just as he had brought Israel out of Egypt (114:1). The restoration transformed the weeping of the Lord’s people into "laughter" and showed the Lord’s character to the "nations" (9:11; 64:9; Isa 12:4).
verses.4-6: The prophets had spoken of the restoration as a time when the wilderness would change into the Garden of Eden (Isa 51:3; Ezek 47); the reality fell far short of paradise. Here the restoration community prays for full redemption (see Hag 2:19). • "as streams renew the desert:" The seasonal rains filled the dry river beds (wadis), and the land turned green again. The prayer looks for a similar transformation of Israel’s "fortunes", a fulfillment of the imagery of the “Second Exodus” in Isaiah (see “The Promise of a Second Exodus” Theme Note). • The "harvest" represents God’s full restoration.

verses.1-5: Blessing and protection come from God. Without his presence, there is no success (127:1-2). This is particularly true for children, who are God’s gift (127:3-5).
verses.1-2: "Unless:" These conditional sentences emphasize the positive idea that the Lord will protect the city (cp. 124:1-2). • Human effort is futile unless the Lord blesses it (see 44:3). • "from early morning until late at night:" This depicts an aggressive and competitive lifestyle. • God’s "loved ones" enjoy a quiet night’s sleep (3:5; 4:8).
verses.3-5: "Children" are one of God’s blessings. The words translated “children” (Hebrew banim) and “builders” (bonim, 127:1) form a wordplay. Having children builds a family.
verses.4-5: "like arrows:" God uses children to protect the reputation of his people against the wicked (cp. 120:4; 7:12-13).

verses.3: Like "vigorous young olive trees", children are saplings filled with potential. Olive oil symbolizes God’s blessing (104:15; Num 18:12; Jer 31:12; Hag 2:19).
verses.1-6: The godly, who fear the Lord, will know true happiness (128:1-2). The Lord is with them (see 127:1-2), building their home life (128:3-4) and blessing them across the generations (128:5-6).
verses.1-2: Enjoying "the fruit" of one’s "labor" means gaining benefit from whatever work one does.
verses.4-6: God will "continually bless" all who fear him (133:3) from his dwelling in "Zion" (20:2; 50:2; 110:2), no matter where they live. • "grandchildren:" God’s blessings extend from generation to generation for the faithful (79:12-13; 89:1; 100:4-5; 103:17-19).

verses.1-8: The psalmist briefly reviews Israel’s history of trouble (129:1-2) and redemption (129:3-4). He concludes with curses against the enemies and blessings on the godly (129:5-6).
verses.1-2: Israel’s "earliest youth" as a nation was during its sojourn in Egypt.
verses.3-4: "the" Lord" is good:" He rescued Israel from Egypt, from many enemy attacks, and from the Babylonian exile.
verses.6-8: "Grass on a rooftop" had shallow roots and would scorch easily. A crop was "ignored by the harvester" when the yield was low. The enemies who had sown hurt among God’s people would gain little.

verses.3: The psalmist knows that his "sins" make him guilty and deserving of God’s judgment.
verses.5: God’s "word" imparts "hope" (119:42-43, 49; 147:11).
verses.1-8: Beginning with himself as a representative of the community, the psalmist cries for God’s mercy (130:1-3) out of deep distress. He places his hope in the Lord (130:4-6), knowing that the Lord will rescue when and as he chooses. Based on this confidence, the psalmist invites Israel to wait for the Lord (130:7-8).
verses.1-3: A "cry" from "the depths" is from a place of deep distress (cp. 69:2, 14; Isa 51:10; Ezek 27:34). Out of the frailty of his being, the psalmist prays for divine favor.
verses.4-6: The good news comes in God’s readiness to forgive sinners. His grace encourages people to fear him and hope in him.
verses.7-8: "Israel" is invited to "hope in the "Lord (9:18; 27:14; 131:3) because the Lord pays the costly price for "redemption" and covers whatever "sin" separates humans from him (see also 111:9; Exod 6:6-8; 2 Sam 7:23-24; Isa 43:1-4; Titus 2:14; Heb 9:12; 1 Pet 1:18).

verses.1: The "heart" represents the whole being (see 27:8). • God hates arrogance, which is a foolish way of life (Prov 6:16-19). • The psalmist does not trouble himself with matters that properly belong to the Lord.
verses.2: The psalmist "calmed and quieted" himself, surrendering his ambitions and taming his ego (Gal 2:20). • "like a weaned child:" The psalmist sees himself as a contented child.
verses.1-3: Out of his contentment in the Lord, the psalmist invites Israel to seek their rest in God (131:3).

verses.6: "Ephrathah" is Bethlehem (Gen 35:19; 48:7). • "Jaar" is the singular form of the plural “Jearim.” The Ark was at Kiriath-jearim for twenty years in Samuel’s time (1 Sam 7:1-2).
verses.9: The "priests" were to exhibit righteousness in their lives (132:16; Mal 2:6).
verses.17: "anointed one:" The ruler God chose and established (see Pss 1–8) would never cease to provide "light for" the Lord’s "people." This light would burn continually (see 1 Kgs 11:36; 2 Kgs 8:19; cp. John 8:12; Rev 21:23-24).
verses.18: The adversaries will be humiliated, in contrast to the "glorious king" (132:9, 16).
verses.1-18: This psalm celebrates the Lord’s faithfulness to David. When David wanted to bring the Ark into Jerusalem (132:1-5), the Lord granted the request and made Jerusalem his earthly home (132:6-10). The choice of Jerusalem marked God’s election of David’s line (132:11-13), of Zion (132:14-17), and of the priesthood (132:9, 16).
verses.6-10: These verses form a recollection of David’s moving the Ark of the Covenant to Jerusalem (2 Sam 6:1-15) and of the Lord’s oath to David (2 Sam 7:4-16).
verses.8-10: These verses are a quotation from Solomon’s prayer at the dedication of the Temple (2 Chr 6:41-42).
verses.11-12: The Lord" swore an oath to David" (2 Sam 7:4-16): God’s "promise" is unconditional, but the covenant is not ("If . . . then"). Those who break God’s covenant can expect the discipline of God’s judgment (see Ps 89:30-37).
verses.13-17: The psalmist recounts the selection of Jerusalem and of the priests.

verses.1: "Brothers" are related by blood, by profession, or by commitment.
verses.2: The "anointing oil" was the oil used to ordain and consecrate Aaron for service in his office (see Exod 29:7). • "head . . . beard . . . border of his robe:" The oil consecrated Aaron completely.
verses.3: The "dew" represents the richness of divine blessings; in Jerusalem, it comes from moist winds from the Mediterranean Sea. "Mount Hermon", which is capped with snow, is a place of abundant moisture. • A "blessing" is God’s life-giving power, a guarantee of his provision and protection (5:12; 41:2), secured by his presence (21:6; 67:1). Even the other nations will ultimately be blessed (Pss 67; 72:17). Zion is the focal point of God’s blessing (134:3; 147:13). • God gives "life everlasting" to human beings.
verses.1-3: In this wisdom psalm (see Ps 1), peaceful and harmonious relationships manifest the presence of God.
verses.1-2: The psalmist tells of the joy of consecrated relationships.

verses.1-3: In the last of the pilgrims’ songs (Pss 120–134), the travelers call the Temple workers to praise the Lord. In return, they will receive a much-anticipated blessing.
verses.1-2: Those "who serve at night" were the priests and Levites (see also 135:2).

verses.4: The synonyms "Jacob" and "Israel" include all twelve tribes. The Lord cherishes his chosen people. They are his "treasure" out of all the kingdoms of the world (Exod 19:5-6).
verses.5: The Lord is superior to any real or imagined supernatural being (see 95:3-5; 115:4-8).
verses.6: God is sovereign over the whole created order—he "does whatever pleases him" him. • The phrase "heaven and earth" refers to all of creation.
verses.7: The psalmist tells of God’s sovereignty over the weather (Pss 29; 77:17-18; 78:26; 104:4; 147:8-9; 148:5-6).
verses.1-21: God, the Creator and the Lord of history, “made heaven and earth” (134:3). He deserves praise because, unlike idols, he redeems his people.
verses.8-12: The Lord was sovereign over the Exodus and the conquest of the Promised Land.
verses.8-11: In the tenth and culminating plague against Egypt, God "destroyed the firstborn" of each family. • The "miraculous signs and wonders" are the ten plagues (see Exod 7–11; Deut 4:34; Neh 9:10).
verses.13-18: The Lord’s name and character stand in contrast to idols.
verses.15-20: This entire section is repeated in 115:4-11.
verses.15-18: Idols corrupt the thinking because they are "merely things" made by humans; they cannot "speak, see, hear," or "breathe" (Isa 41:22-24; 44:9, 18; Rom 1:21-23).
verses.19-21: The groups named here comprised the covenant community (see 115:9-11).

verses.25: The Lord provides for all of his creatures.
verses.26: The phrase "God of heaven" is an exilic and postexilic designation for the Lord; it is found in Ezra (Ezra 1:2; 5:11, 12; 6:9, 10; 7:12; etc.), Nehemiah (Neh 1:5; 2:4, 20; etc.), and Daniel (Dan 2:18, 19, 37, 44).
verses.1-26: This is the last of the Great Hallel psalms (Pss 120–136). It distinctively repeats the refrain "His faithful love endures forever" in every verse.
